title: Prologue — The Whisper Beneath the Thorne
content:
The throne room had stopped breathing.

Mireille noticed it in the way the candlelight no longer danced along the walls. The flames stood still as held breath, their amber tongues reaching but never quite touching the vaulted stone above. The air itself had thickened, carrying the mineral sweetness of deep earth and something older beneath it—something that tasted of bruised iron and the first frost of a winter that never arrived.

She had been sitting on the Throne of Thorns for longer than she could remember today. The marks on her forearms pulsed in slow, arrhythmic time with a heartbeat that was not her own. They were beautiful in the way a wound is beautiful when it has become part of the landscape of your body: silver-white lines branching like frost-fern across her skin, tracing paths from wrist to elbow and climbing the soft underside of her forearm in delicate, barbed whorls. The Throne gave her these marks in exchange for what she could no longer name.

The Crown of Echoes rested against her temples with the weight of centuries. It did not feel like a crown anymore. It felt like the pressure of deep water, the way the ocean presses against the hull of a sunken ship—constant, patient, and absolutely indifferent to the thing it was slowly consuming.

She closed her eyes and let the silence fill her.

From somewhere far below her feet—beneath the obsidian floor, beneath the roots of the caldera, beneath three hundred years of slow and catastrophic unraveling—the Rootsong hummed.

It was not the sound it had once been. Mireille remembered when the Rootsong had been a chorus, when it had risen from the earth like spring water, clear and bright and full of names. Now it was a single thread of sound, thin as spider silk and just as fragile, vibrating at a frequency that made her teeth ache and the hollows behind her eyes fill with something that was not quite pain. It was the sound of a heart that had forgotten how to beat in rhythm, each pulse arriving a fraction of a second too late, as though the earth itself had begun to stutter.

And beneath the stutter, the whisper.

It had been whispering to her for so long that she had stopped being able to distinguish the moments when it began from the moments when it ended. It was always there, threading through the silence between her thoughts, surfacing in the gaps between her breaths. A name. Always the same name. A human name, spoken in a language that predated the courts, predated the Sundering, predated the very stone she sat upon.

Seren.

Mireille opened her eyes.

The throne room stretched before her, and for a moment she saw it the way it must have looked in the early centuries—when the Court of Dusk and Bramble was not a ruin wrapped in thorns but a living architecture of obsidian and moonstone, its corridors lit by bioluminescent moss and its chambers fragrant with night-blooming jasmine. She could almost see the way the banners had hung from the vaulted ceiling, each one bearing the sigil of a household that no longer existed. She could almost hear the murmur of a court that had numbered in the thousands, voices overlapping in the old tongue, laughter rising like incense toward the domed ceiling where stained glass filtered the last light of the Vaelthorn sun into colours that had no names in any human language.

Then the vision shifted, the way it always did, like a reflection in disturbed water.

The banners were gone. Not fallen—consumed. Where they had hung, the walls bore the blackened imprints of their fabric, ghost-shapes marking the places where colour had been. The moss on the walls had turned grey and brittle, flaking to the floor in small, ashen drifts. The jasmine had been dead for decades, and in its place the air carried only the mineral tang of stone dissolution and the faintly sweet, utterly alien scent of the Thornwall.

Mireille turned her head slowly toward the eastern window.

It was there.

The Thornwall had been creeping closer for years—she thought it was years, though time had become unreliable since the Crown began eating her memories in earnest—but today it was closer than she remembered. A tangle of dark vines, each one as thick as her wrist, had climbed the outer wall of the throne room and pressed against the ancient glass like a hand pressing against the surface of a frozen lake. The thorns were the colour of dried blood, each one curved and serrated, and they caught the last of the dying light and held it in their tips so that for a moment the wall seemed to be studded with small, malevolent gems.

Behind the glass, the vine-work was already inside. She could see where the thorns had punched through the mortar between the stones, their dark roots threading through cracks that should not have been there, should not have been wide enough. They moved with the slow, patient certainty of something that knew it had all the time in the world. Which it did. Because the world was running out.

A section of the outer corridor—that beautiful, arched corridor that had once connected the throne room to the Hall of Petals—had been swallowed entirely. Mireille tried to remember the last time she had walked that corridor. She tried to remember who had been with her. There had been someone. She was certain there had been someone. A face hovered at the edge of her recall, familiar and beloved, but before she could focus on it the memory dissolved like smoke, leaving only the hollow ache of its absence.

* * *

She pressed her hand flat against the arm of the Throne. The stone was warm—warmer than it should have been, warmer than stone ever was. The Throne was connected to the Rootsong, and the Rootsong was failing, and the warmth was not the warmth of life but the warmth of a fever, the heat of something burning from the inside out.

The whisper came again, stronger this time, insistent.

Seren.

Mireille drew a breath. It rattled in her chest, and she was startled by how thin it sounded, how much it resembled the sound of the Rootsong itself—a single thread, stretched to its limit, vibrating in the space between being and ceasing to be.

“How long?” she asked the empty room.

The question was not new. She had asked it a thousand times, or perhaps ten thousand, in this room that had stopped breathing. How long until the Rootsong falls silent? How long until the Thornwall consumes the last of the Court? How long until I forget my own name, the way I have forgotten everything else?

The room did not answer. The Rootsong did not answer. The Crown of Echoes pressed against her temples and offered her only the sound of her own heartbeat, which was no longer entirely her own.

But the whisper persisted.

Seren.

It was not a warning. It was not a summons. It was something far older and far more patient than either of those things. It was the sound of a door opening slowly, the way doors open in dreams—without sound, without effort, revealing a room that had always been there, waiting.

Mireille lifted her hand from the Throne and looked at the thorn-marks on her palm. They traced the lines of her fate in a language she had once been able to read. Now they were just marks—beautiful, meaningless, permanent.

She thought of the name the Rootsong had been whispering for three centuries. She thought of the way it felt when the whisper was strongest—not like a sound but like a hook behind her sternum, a gentle, inexorable pull toward something she could not see.

* * *

The human is coming.

The thought arrived not as words but as a certainty, blooming in the space where a memory used to be. She did not know how she knew it. She did not know what it meant. But she knew it the way she knew her own name—or had known it, before the Crown began its slow harvest.

Mireille rose from the Throne of Thorns. The movement cost her more than it should have; her knees protested, and for a moment the throne room tilted around her, the walls pressing inward like the hull of a sinking ship. She steadied herself against the armrest and felt the thorn-marks on her forearm pulse in response, warm and alive and utterly indifferent to her suffering.

She walked toward the eastern window. The Thornwall watched her come with its thousand thorn-eyes, each one holding a dying point of light. Behind the black tangle, she could see the distant silhouette of the mountain rim, and above it, the sky that had been the colour of ash for as long as she could remember. But tonight—and she was certain it was tonight, though she could not have said why—there was something different about the sky. A thinning at the edges, perhaps. A sense of vastness where there had been only weight.

A vine shifted against the glass. The sound it made was not the creak of wood or the scrape of stone but something closer to a breath drawn through teeth—the slow, wet intake of a thing that was feeding. Beyond the window, a section of the inner wall that had stood since the court was young crumbled inward without sound, and the thorns rushed in to fill the space it left, dark fingers threading through pale stone the way roots thread through soil.

Mireille watched it happen and felt nothing. Not grief, not rage, not the desperate defiance that had sustained her for the first century of the dying. Only a vast, incurious exhaustion that sat in her chest like a stone, and beneath it, the whisper. The whisper that had never stopped.

She placed her palm against the glass. It was cold, and through it she could feel the Thornwall pulsing—a slow, vegetal heartbeat, rhythmic and patient, utterly unlike the stuttering irregularity of the Rootsong. The two rhythms coexisted in her body: the failing pulse of the deep earth and the steady, encroaching pulse of the thing that was consuming it. They were not at war. They were not enemies. They were simply two forces moving in opposite directions, and she was the territory between them.

The Crown of Echoes pressed harder against her temples, and a memory surfaced—brief, luminous, gone before she could hold it. A garden. Moonlight. The scent of jasmine so thick it was almost a flavour. Hands holding hers, and a voice saying something she could not hear. Then the glass shattered in her mind, and the garden was gone, and there was only the cold window and the thorns pressing against it from the other side, and the endless, patient whisper threading through the wreckage of a memory she would never recover.

She let her hand fall to her side.

“Soon,” she said. The word was not a promise. It was not a prayer. It was the simple acknowledgment of something she had felt in the marrow of her bones for longer than she could remember counting. The stalemate was ending. The door was opening. The name that the Rootsong had carried through three centuries of silence and decay was no longer just a whisper on the wind.

It was an arrival.

* * *

The whisper swelled, and for the first time in three hundred years, it was not merely a name.

It was a beginning.

Seren.

title: Chapter 1 — The Crossing
content:
The bookshop on HeolMaengwyn was supposed to open at nine. It usually opened at nine-fifteen, because Dafydd Meredith had never met a schedule he couldn’t be personally offended by. The building had been, at various points in its long and structurally dubious life, a butcher’s, a chapel, and — if Dafydd was to be believed, which he rarely was — a brothel. Seren suspected he’d invented the brothel story entirely, because it earned him free pints at the Owain Glyndwr and gave tourists a reason to buy the overpriced local history books he kept by the till.

She’d been working there for three years. Part-time at first, when the English degree she’d spent four years acquiring qualified her for precisely nothing except a keen awareness of how underpaid she was. Then full-time, when it became apparent that the bookshop was the only place in Machynlleth where she could spend eight hours a day without someone asking her how she was really doing. Books didn’t ask questions. They just sat there, being themselves, which was more than she could say for most people.

The shop smelled of old paper and damp wool and the particular mustiness that accumulated in places where time moved slower than the world outside. The shelves were crammed so tight that removing a book from the middle of a row was an act of structural engineering. Dafydd sorted by mood rather than category, which meant the Victorian poetry lived next to the car repair manuals and the Welsh cookbooks were shelved beside a dog-eared copy of Fifty Shades of Grey that no one had ever bought and no one had the heart to throw away.

She’d developed a system for the shelves, inasmuch as anything Dafydd touched could be called a system. She’d put sticky notes on the sections: FICTION, HISTORY, WILDLIFE, WELSH, WEIRD STUFF DAFYDD WON’T EXPLAIN. That last category was the largest. It contained books on ley lines, Celtic mythology, and one very old volume bound in something that might have been leather but felt, disconcertingly, like bark. Dafydd had told her not to touch that one. She’d touched it anyway, late one evening when the shop was empty, and it had done something to the overhead light that she still couldn’t explain and had decided, firmly, not to think about.

She was reorganising the Wales section — a futile task, since Dafydd would reshuffle everything the moment her back was turned — when the bell above the door chimed and Mrs. Griffiths entered with the particular expression of a woman who had come for something other than books.

“Bore da, cariad,” Mrs. Griffiths said, which meant good morning and also I have information about you. “Lovely day, isn’t it?”

It was not a lovely day. It was Tuesday in Machynlleth, which meant the sky was the colour of wet slate and the rain had settled in for the duration, the way it always did, with the quiet determination of something that had nowhere else to be.

“Stunning,” Seren said. “Peak Wales.”

Mrs. Griffiths beamed, either missing the irony or choosing to, and began her circuit of the shop. She picked up a book, examined its spine, replaced it. Picked up another. She was circling. Seren could tell because Mrs. Griffiths always circled before she struck, like a heron sizing up a fish.

“Your father was in the Spar yesterday,” Mrs. Griffiths said, with the elaborate casualness of someone who had been waiting to say this since before she’d walked through the door. “Looking well, he is. Considering.”

Considering. That was a loaded word in Machynlleth. Considering covered everything from his health to his drinking to the fact that he lived alone in a house that was slowly emptying of furniture, one room at a time, as though the house itself was grieving something it couldn’t name.

“He does look well,” Seren said. She shelved a book on the history of Ceredigion. “Thanks for the update.”

“And how are you keeping, love? Still on your own up at Eira’s old place?”

Eira’s old place. The cottage on the hill that Seren’s grandmother had left her when she died, twelve years ago, along with a lifetime of questions that Seren had carefully not asked. The cottage smelled like lavender and dust and the ghost of a woman who had known things she’d never told anyone. Seren had grown up in that cottage. She’d learned to read in its kitchen. She’d cried in its garden after her mother left, though she’d never told anyone about that, because saying it out loud would have made it real, and Seren had very firm opinions about which things deserved to be real.

“The cottage is fine,” Seren said. “I’m fine. Everything’s fine.”

She said this with the specific inflection that meant nothing was fine, and Mrs. Griffiths heard it with the specific hearing that meant she wasn’t going to push, because pushing Seren Ashwood was like pushing a wall — technically possible, but deeply unrewarding.

“Your mother’s birthday is coming up, isn’t it?” Mrs. Griffiths added, as she was leaving. She said it casually, the way people said things they knew would land like stones in still water. “Seventeen years since she—”

“Thanks for the reminder,” Seren said. “Have a lovely afternoon.”

Mrs. Griffiths bought a bookmark. She lingered. She left. The bell chimed behind her, and the shop settled back into its quiet, and Seren let out a breath she hadn’t realised she’d been holding.

She stood behind the counter, hands flat on the wood, and looked out the window at HeolMaengwyn. The rain streaked the glass in long, wandering lines, like something trying to write a message it couldn’t quite finish. The street was empty except for a dog standing in a doorway, looking profoundly betrayed by the weather.

Machynlleth was a market town of about two thousand people, most of whom had known each other since birth and all of whom knew Seren’s business better than she did. It sat in a bowl of hills in the Dyfi Valley, grey stone and greyer sky, the river threading through it like a vein. It was beautiful, if you liked that sort of thing — the wild emptiness of mid-Wales, the way the hills closed in like cupped hands, the quality of the light when the sun finally bothered to show itself, gilding everything in a thin, improbable gold. Seren did like that sort of thing. She’d never admitted it to anyone, because admitting you liked something in Machynlleth was an invitation for people to Expect Things, and Seren had enough expectations riding on her without adding any more.

* * *

Mei Thornton arrived at half past twelve, the way she always did — through the door without knocking, already talking, holding two paper cups from the café across the street like they were offerings to a particularly demanding god.

“Chai latte,” she said, setting one on the counter. “And before you ask, yes, it’s got the oat milk, and no, I didn’t fight the barista about it this time. I made a stern face and he respected my authority.”

“You made a stern face at a nineteen-year-old called Dylan.”

“A nineteen-year-old called Dylan who has been putting cow’s milk in my chai for three weeks despite my repeated requests. There are only so many times a woman can explain the concept of oat milk before she resorts to facial expressions.”

Seren took the cup. It was warm, and it tasted like autumn and compromise, and she drank it without comment because commenting would have meant having a feeling about Mei remembering her order, and feelings were things Seren dealt with the way she dealt with the leak in the cottage roof — by pretending they didn’t exist until they became impossible to ignore.

Mei was twenty-four, worked at the veterinary practice on the high street, and had been Seren’s best friend since they were eleven and Mei had punched Gethin Price in the nose for calling Seren a freak. They’d been inseparable since, though “inseparable” was a generous word for what they actually were, which was two people who recognised something broken in each other and had decided, for reasons neither of them fully understood, not to walk away from it.

Mei was the warmest person Seren had ever met. Not in a performative, look-at-me-being-nice way, but in the way of someone who simply could not help caring about people, even when those people — specifically, one person — made it extremely difficult. She had dark hair she wore in a messy bun, paint under her fingernails from the watercolours she did in her spare time, and the kind of smile that made strangers want to tell her their problems. Which they did, constantly. Mei collected other people’s sadness the way other people collected ceramic frogs. She had a flat above the charity shop that was permanently full of stray animals she was ‘just looking after until we find them homes,’ a situation that had been going on for so long that she now owned, by any reasonable definition, four cats and a cockatiel called Dave.

They talked about nothing for a while — Mei’s job, a dog that had eaten a sock, the new bus timetable that no one had asked for and everyone hated. The shop was quiet. The rain had moved from drizzle to something more committed. Outside, the hills had disappeared into cloud, and Machynlleth felt less like a town and more like the last room in a very large house, the one where the walls were closing in.

Then Mei’s face did the thing it did when she was working up to something serious — a slight tightening around the eyes, a pause in the rhythm of her talking, as though she was shifting gears internally.

“Right,” Mei said. “I need to tell you something, and you’re going to be annoying about it, but I’m telling you anyway.”

“I’m never annoying. I’m delightful. I’m a joy.”

“You’re a nightmare in a cardigan.”

“This cardigan is vintage.”

Mei took a breath. “I went to the storage unit. The one with your nan’s things in it — the stuff from the cottage you never went through.”

The temperature in the shop dropped by several degrees, or at least it felt that way. Seren set down her chai latte with the careful precision of someone who was trying very hard not to throw it.

“Which storage unit,” Seren said, “would that be.”

“The one in Dolgellau. Your nan’s papers, the old books, the boxes from the attic. The ones you’ve been ignoring for twelve years.”

“I haven’t been ignoring them. I’ve been strategically not dealing with them. There’s a difference.”

“Seren.”

“Mei.”

They looked at each other. Mei’s expression was the one she wore when she was about to say something that was going to hurt but needed to be said anyway. It was an expression Seren had seen approximately four hundred times since they were eleven, and it had never once failed to make her want to climb out a window.

“There was a tin,” Mei said, quieter now. “Old tobacco tin, like the ones your nan used to keep in the kitchen. It had papers in it. Letters, mostly. And some drawings — weird symbols, like something out of a history book. There was a map, too, of the valley. But it didn’t look like any map I’ve seen. There were places marked on it that don’t exist. At least, I don’t think they do.”

Seren said nothing. She was aware, in the distant, detached way she was aware of most things that mattered, that her heart was beating faster than it should. Eira had kept things. Eira had always kept things — jam jars and buttons and scraps of paper with Welsh words scrawled on them in her cramped, elegant handwriting. Eira had known things. Seren had understood this as a child the way children understand that water is wet and the sky is high — completely, intuitively, without the words for it. Her grandmother had known things that other people didn’t know, and she had carried those things alone, and when she died she’d taken most of them with her.

“I didn’t read the letters,” Mei added quickly. “They’re yours. I just — I thought you should know. That the tin is there. In case you wanted to—”

“Not today.”

The words came out flat, final, the way a door sounds when it closes. Mei heard the door and did not try to open it. This was the architecture of their friendship — Mei offered, Seren refused, Mei didn’t push, and somehow, against all odds, nothing fell apart.

For a moment neither of them spoke. The rain tapped against the window, and the shop hummed with its quiet, and somewhere in the back of her mind Seren could hear her grandmother’s voice, faint and half-remembered, saying something in Welsh that she’d never understood. Eira had spoken Welsh the way some people spoke music — fluently, instinctively, as though the language lived in her blood rather than her mind. Seren had never learned more than a handful of words. She’d told herself, at twelve, that it was because no one spoke Welsh anymore. The truth was that it sounded too much like her grandmother, and her grandmother was a door Seren had also learned not to open.

“Okay,” Mei said. “Not today. But the tin’s at mine. Whenever you’re ready.”

Seren nodded. She picked up her chai latte and drank half of it in one go, because chai latte was safe and controllable and didn’t require her to have feelings about her dead grandmother’s mysterious papers.

“Walk home together after work?” Mei asked, already knowing the answer.

“Fine.”

“You say that like I’ve asked you to accompany me to a crime scene.”

“I’ve seen the state of your kitchen, Mei. A crime scene is generous.”

Mei threw a bookmark at her. Seren dodged it with the practiced ease of someone who’d been dodging Mei’s bookmarks for thirteen years. The shop settled back into its quiet, and the rain kept falling, and Seren did not think about the tin or the letters or the map with places that didn’t exist, because thinking about those things would mean thinking about Eira, and thinking about Eira meant thinking about all the things her grandmother had never told her, and Seren Ashwood had a very specific policy about things that couldn’t be explained, which was to put them in a box and leave them in a storage unit in Dolgellau and never, ever open them.

* * *

They closed the shop at five. Dafydd had left at four, as he always did, with a vague wave and a promise to do the accounts that they both knew he wouldn’t. Seren locked the door, turned the sign to CLOSED, and stood on the pavement with Mei while the rain did its best to turn them both into watercolours.

The shopfront next door — a charity shop that changed its window display with the enthusiasm of someone who’d just discovered Pinterest — had put out a rack of coats. One of them, a hideous orange thing that looked like it had been knitted by a spiteful aunt, had already blown half into the street. Seren righted it automatically, because she righted things automatically, because someone had to, and if she didn’t do it no one would, and that was the problem with living in a small town where everyone knew everything about everyone: you couldn’t walk past a fallen coat without wondering if Mrs. Griffiths was watching from behind her net curtains, which she almost certainly was.

Machynlleth at dusk was a particular kind of beautiful — the kind that required a certain tolerance for grey. The streetlights flickered on, casting pools of amber on wet stone. The hills had faded to silhouettes, their shapes soft and uncertain against a sky that couldn’t decide between rain and dark. The river Dyfi was somewhere to the west, invisible but audible, a low, constant murmur that threaded through the town like a conversation you could half-hear through a wall.

They walked. This was their routine — bookshop to the high street, high street to the bridge, bridge to the path along the river. Mei talked. Seren listened and said sharp things at intervals. It was a system that worked.

“You know what I think?” Mei said, steering them left toward the river path.

“I dread it, but continue.”

“I think you should talk to your dad.”

“And I think you should mind your own business, but here we are.”

“He’s lonely, Seren. Mrs. Griffiths isn’t the only one who’s noticed.”

Seren didn’t answer immediately. They passed the old chapel, its stone dark with rain, the graveyard behind it tilting gently into the hillside. Her father had taken her there once, when she was small, to visit her mother’s grave. There hadn’t been a grave. There had been a plot of empty earth and a headstone that said her mother’s name but felt, somehow, like a lie. Her father had stood there in silence for twenty minutes, and then they’d gone home, and neither of them had ever gone back.

She said it the way she said everything was fine — with the bright, hard edge of someone who had rehearsed the sentence so many times it had lost all meaning. Mei heard it. Mei always heard it. But Mei also knew that pushing Seren was like pushing a tide — you could stand there and push all you wanted, but the sea was going to do what the sea was going to do.

“My father is a grown man who lives alone by choice. He likes it that way. He has the telly and the garden and a bottle of Jameson’s that seems to refill itself by magic. He’s fine.”

The river path narrowed as they walked. The houses thinned, replaced by fields and hedgerows and the dark, wet shapes of trees. A sheep regarded them with the profound disinterest that only sheep could muster, standing in the rain with the expression of something that had seen humanity’s entire enterprise and found it wanting. Seren had always liked sheep. They had no expectations.

The mist was thick tonight — thicker than usual for October, rolling in off the hills in grey-white ribbons, pooling in the hollows of the land like something settling. It muffled sound, swallowed distance. The streetlights behind them had become vague amber smudges, as though the town was being slowly erased.

“Misty,” Mei observed, pulling her jacket tighter.

“Astute.”

“I’m just saying, it’s thicker than normal. Even for here.”

It was. Seren had noticed it too, in the way she noticed everything — automatically, involuntarily, like breathing. The mist wasn’t moving with the wind. It wasn’t drifting or rolling or doing any of the things mist was supposed to do. It was pooling. Settling. Collecting in specific places — the bends in the path, the gaps in the hedgerows, the low places where the river ran closest to the land — as though it was being drawn there by something.

She said none of this. It was probably nothing. Weather did what it wanted in mid-Wales. The mist was thick, the air was cold, and they were walking along a river at dusk in October, which was exactly the sort of situation where your brain started filling in patterns that weren’t there.

They reached the bend in the river where the path widened into a small clearing — a patch of grass and mud where locals sometimes sat in the summer, though not today, because today the clearing was empty and white and utterly still, and the mist was so thick that Seren could barely see the water ten feet away.

* * *

It started with the sound.

Not a sound, exactly. More like the absence of one — the river, which had been a constant, murmuring presence since they’d left the town, went quiet. Not gradually. All at once, as though someone had laid a hand over the water and stilled it. The silence was immediate and enormous, pressing in on them from all sides, and for a moment the only thing Seren could hear was her own heartbeat and the rain hitting the grass at her feet, which was wrong, because the rain had stopped too, though she hadn’t noticed when.

The temperature dropped.

Not the slow, creeping cold of a Welsh evening settling in. A sudden, sharp drop, like walking into a cold room, like the air itself had been replaced by something denser, older, colder. Seren’s breath misted in front of her face. The ground beneath her feet seemed to vibrate, so faintly she might have imagined it, a low, rhythmic pulse that wasn’t quite a sound and wasn’t quite a feeling, but was somewhere in the space between, like a bass note played too low for human hearing.

“Seren.” Mei’s voice was tight. “Do you feel that?”

Seren felt it. She felt it in her chest, in the hollow space behind her sternum, in the place where she kept all the things she didn’t want to feel. A pull. Not physical — or not entirely physical. Something deeper than muscle and bone. Something that recognised a frequency she didn’t know she could hear. It was pulling her toward the river.

She’d felt something like this before. Headaches, mostly. Sudden, sharp pains that came and went without warning, usually when she was near something old — standing stones, ruined chapels, the old bridge at Dolgellau. She’d mentioned it to her GP once, who’d run tests and found nothing and told her it was probably migraines, and Seren had accepted this explanation with the same pragmatic indifference she applied to most things that couldn’t be fixed by tea and stubbornness.

This was not a headache.

The mist parted.

Not naturally — not the way mist parts when the wind catches it, thinning and stretching and dissolving. This was deliberate. The mist drew aside like a curtain, revealing the river in a corridor of white-grey air, and for a moment Seren could see the Dyfi clearly — the dark water, the far bank, the black shapes of the trees beyond. And in the water, threading through the current like veins through the back of a hand, she saw something that was not river.

Thorns.

Dark, curved shapes rising from the riverbed, lacing through the water in patterns that were too deliberate to be natural. They were the colour of dried blood, each one curved and serrated, and they pulsed — actually pulsed, in slow, rhythmic time, like a heartbeat made visible. The water around them was darker, thicker, as though whatever they were was bleeding into the river, staining it.

Above the thorns, in the mist, a shape.

It wasn’t a tree. It wasn’t a building. It wasn’t anything that belonged in this world, in this river, in this mist. It was vast and dark and alive, pressing against the boundary of reality the way a face presses against glass — distorting, warping, filling the mist with the impression of something enormous and patient and desperately, hungrily aware.

Seren heard the whisper.

It wasn’t in her ears. It was in her bones, in the blood, in the space behind her sternum where the pull had been. A sound that was almost a name, spoken by something ancient and enormous and dying, reaching across a distance that shouldn’t have been possible.

Seren.

She didn’t freeze. She didn’t scream. She didn’t do any of the things that sensible people did when confronted with something that shouldn’t exist. What she did was get angry.

“What the fuck is that?”

Her voice cracked through the silence like a stone through glass. She stepped forward — toward the river, toward the thorns, toward the vast and impossible shape in the mist — because Seren Ashwood’s first response to something terrifying was not to run but to confront it, because running meant admitting she was afraid, and admitting she was afraid meant admitting she was small, and Seren had spent twenty-four years refusing to be small.

Mei grabbed her arm. “Seren, don—”

The shape in the mist surged forward. The thorns in the river convulsed. The air pressure changed — a sudden, violent compression, like the sky itself was inhaling — and then everything snapped.

The mist closed. The sound rushed back in — the river, the wind, the distant hum of the town — and the world was exactly as it had been. Grey, wet, October-cold. The path beneath their feet. The trees behind them. The river in front of them, dark and fast-flowing and completely, utterly ordinary. No thorns. No shape. No whisper. Just the Dyfi, doing what the Dyfi had always done, which was flow toward the sea with the quiet persistence of water that had nowhere else to go.

Mei was holding Seren’s arm so tightly her fingers would leave marks. Her face was white. “Seren. Seren, what was that? What the fuck was that?”

Seren couldn’t answer. She was staring at the riverbank. At the ground where she’d been standing when the pull was strongest.

The grass was blackened.

A perfect circle of dead, blackened grass, three feet across, on the muddy bank of the River Dyfi where five seconds ago there had been nothing but mud and rain and the ordinary, unremarkable ground of mid-Wales. The edges of the circle were sharp and clean, as though something had pressed down there with enormous, focused weight. The grass within it was not merely dead — it was flattened, compressed, as though crushed by something that had stood in that exact spot and then vanished.

Mei saw it too. She made a small, wounded sound that was not quite a word.

Seren crouched. Her knees were shaking, which was inconvenient and annoying and absolutely not something she was going to acknowledge. She reached out toward the blackened grass and stopped an inch above it. The air above the circle was cold. Not October cold. Stone cold. The kind of cold that came from deep underground, from centuries of darkness and pressure, from places where the sun had never reached.

Then she saw the thorn.

It was pushing up through the mud at the edge of the blackened circle, no bigger than her little finger, dark as dried blood and curved like a claw. It had a serrated edge, each tooth precise and deliberate, and it was growing — actually growing, visibly, pushing up through the earth like something surfacing.

She knew, with the same absolute, irrefutable certainty she knew her own name, that it shouldn’t exist. Not here. Not in this world. Not in the mud of the River Dyfi on a Tuesday evening in Machynlleth. But there it was, dark and real and alive, and it was looking at her. Not with eyes, because it didn’t have eyes, but with something worse — with attention. With recognition.

“Seren.” Mei’s voice was barely a whisper. “Don’t touch it.”

Seren reached for it.

It was warm.

Not the warmth of something recently in the sun — there hadn’t been sun for days. Not the warmth of decay or chemistry or any process she could name. It was warm the way a living thing is warm, warm the way skin is warm, warm with the steady, patient heat of something that had been alive for a very long time and intended to keep being alive for a great deal longer.

And in the moment her fingers closed around it, something shifted inside her. Not the pull — the pull was still there, still humming in her chest like a second heartbeat — but something else. Something deeper. Like a key turning in a lock she hadn’t known existed. Like a door opening in a wall she’d spent her entire life building, and on the other side of that door was a room she’d been pretending wasn’t there, and the room was full of things she didn’t have words for yet.

The thorn crumbled.

Not broke — crumbled, turning to fine, black dust in her palm, as though it had been waiting for her touch and her touch alone, and now that it had been touched it was done, its purpose fulfilled. The dust was warm too, and it clung to her skin, sinking into the lines of her palm like it was trying to get inside her.

Seren stood up. Her hand was trembling. She looked at Mei, who was staring at her with an expression that contained approximately equal parts terror and something that looked horribly like recognition.

“Seren Thornton Ashwood.” Mei used her full name, which meant she was serious. “What the fuck was that.”

Seren looked at her palm. The black dust was gone — absorbed, or evaporated, or simply no longer there. The skin of her palm looked normal. But the warmth remained, a faint, steady pulse in the centre of her hand, beating in time with the pull in her chest, and she understood, with the same gut-level certainty that she understood hunger and tiredness and love, that something had changed. Something had opened. And it was not going to close.

“I don’t know,” she said.

She said it quietly, without the shield of sarcasm, without the sharp edge she used to keep people at a distance. For perhaps the first time since she was seven years old and standing in the doorway of her grandmother’s cottage, watching her mother walk away down the hill in the rain, Seren Ashwood had no walls left to hide behind.

The river murmured. The mist closed in. And somewhere, on the other side of a boundary that shouldn’t exist, something ancient and dying whispered her name one more time, and this time she heard it clearly, and it sounded like a door that had been waiting three hundred years to open.

title: Chapter 2 — The Grey Wing
content:
She didn't sleep.

The warmth in her palm — the thorn’s warmth, the one that had sunk into her skin like it belonged there — kept her awake. Not burning. Not pain. A pulse. Steady and insistent, matching the rhythm of her heartbeat, or perhaps her heartbeat had learned to match it. She lay in the narrow bed in Eira’s cottage and stared at the ceiling and felt the pull in her chest — faint, constant, the way a sound becomes part of the silence after a while.

The cottage was dark. The rain had stopped at some point in the small hours, leaving the kind of silence that pressed against the windows like something curious. She could hear the house settling — the creak of old beams, the tick of cooling stone, all the small protests of a building that had been standing longer than the town around it. She had grown up here. She knew every sound it made.

This was not one of them.

It started as warmth. The same warmth she had felt on the riverbank, when the mist had parted and the thorns had risen from the riverbed like veins — but stronger now, deeper, pulling not at her attention but at something underneath it. At her centre. At the space behind her sternum where the thorn’s dust had settled.

She sat up. The air in the cottage felt wrong. Too still. Too heavy. The darkness did not look like darkness — it looked like something pretending to be darkness, a skin stretched over something else. She could see the outline of her wardrobe, the shape of the door, the rectangle of the window where moonlight should have been. There was no moonlight. There was something else. Something that shifted when she wasn’t looking directly at it, a faint luminescence that was the wrong colour — not silver, not gold, something between, like light that had forgotten what it was supposed to be.

The pull became a tug.

She swung her legs out of bed and her feet touched the floor and the floor was warm. Not the warmth of a heated room — the warmth of something alive, something vast and slow and patient beneath the stone. She had felt this before. Not here. At the standing stones on the hill above Dolgellau, when she was sixteen. At the ruined chapel in the valley, when she was twenty. Always warmth. Always a pull she couldn’t explain and had trained herself to ignore.

She couldn’t ignore this.

The pull was not patient anymore. It was urgent, demanding, a hand around the base of her spine — no, around something deeper than her spine, something she didn’t have a word for. It was pulling her toward the door. Not the front door. The back door. The one that led to the garden, and beyond the garden, to the hill, and beyond the hill — the thorn. The thorn she had touched on the riverbank. The warmth in her palm flared and she looked down and in the dark she could see it — faintly, impossibly, the outline of branching lines on her skin where the dust had settled, like a tattoo drawn in light.

“What the fuck,” she whispered.

The pull yanked.

Not metaphorically. Physically. Her body moved without her permission — not gently, not smoothly, but like something had grabbed her by the ribcage and dragged. Her hand shot out and caught the doorframe and her fingers screamed against the wood and the pull kept going and she was holding on and the thing inside her chest was pulling and the cottage was pulling and the floor was tilting and —

She let go.

The world tore open.

Not a door. Not a window. Not anything she had a frame of reference for. The air in front of her split — a wound in the fabric of everything — and through the wound came light. Wrong light. Amber and bruise-purple and a deep, living green that hurt to look at, and sound — a sound that was not a sound, more like a pressure, a vibration in her teeth and her bones and the marrow of her spine, and cold, not October cold, not Wales cold, but the cold of deep underground places where the sun had never reached.

She was falling.

Not down. Through. Through the wound in the air, through a space that had no dimensions, no up or down, no left or right — just pressure and light and the scream of something enormous and alive all around her. She couldn’t breathe. The air here was different — thicker, denser, tasting of mineral and iron and something older, something that coated the inside of her mouth and throat like the taste of blood. Her ears popped. Her eyes watered. The pull in her chest was the only fixed point in a universe that had become noise and light and vertigo, and she held onto it the way a drowning person holds onto rope, not because she understood it but because it was the only thing that was real.

Then the ground hit her.

Not the ground of the cottage. Not the hill behind the cottage. Not anything she had ever touched. This ground was dark and soft and alive, yielding under her hands when she pushed herself up, and when she looked at her fingers they were stained with something dark — not mud, not earth, but something that glistened faintly, like wet ink.

She was on her hands and knees in a world that was not hers.

The sky was wrong.

That was the first coherent thought she managed, and it was inadequate in the way that “the ocean is large” is inadequate when you are drowning in it. The sky was not the sky she knew. It was vast — too vast, a dome of bruised amber and deep purple that arched overhead like the inside of something enormous and dying, and it had no sun. The light came from everywhere and nowhere, a diffuse amber glow that made the landscape look like a painting left in a fire — all gold and shadow and the deep red-black of char. The horizon was ringed by shapes she couldn’t process — mountains, maybe, but wrong, their peaks shrouded in mist that moved against the wind. To the west, something that looked like a wall, black and vast and alive, made of things that looked like thorns the size of trees, and it was moving, actually moving, growing, advancing across the landscape with the slow patience of something that had been eating this world for centuries and had no intention of stopping.

The air tasted of iron and something else. Something green and rotting and alive. Every breath felt like drinking. The sounds were wrong too — echoes that arrived too late, or too early, distances that didn’t match what her eyes told her. A sound like a bird cried somewhere and the cry came from three directions at once and none of them.

She was in a plain. Grey-green grass that wasn’t grass — the blades were dark, almost black, and they moved when there was no wind, rippling in slow waves away from the west, away from the wall of living thorns. The ground beneath her was warm. Not sun-warm. Something-warm. She pushed herself up to her knees and then to her feet and her legs were shaking, and she was shaking, and her hand was warm, and the pull in her chest had become a direction — east, or what she decided to call east, because the sky here had no sun and she had no compass and the only fixed point she had was the thing inside her that said this way, this way, this way.

“No,” she said out loud, to no one, to the alien sky and the moving grass and the impossible wall. “No. I don’t accept this. I don’t accept any of this.”

The pull didn’t care what she accepted.

It dragged her forward. Not gently — in sharp, staccato tugs, like something that had been waiting a very long time and had finally run out of patience. She stumbled across the grey plain, her feet finding the dark grass, the ground warm beneath her, the air thick in her lungs, and the sky pressing down like a lid on a box she couldn’t open. She tripped on something that might have been a root or might have been nothing and caught herself and kept going because stopping felt like dying and going felt like dying and the only difference was that going was at least moving.

The grass gave way to stone. Dark stone, cracked and veined with something that glowed faintly, like phosphorescence, like the inside of a cave she had visited on a school trip once, except this was not a cave and this was not Wales and she was not eleven anymore and no one was coming to find her. She stopped. Her chest was heaving. The warmth in her palm was a furnace now, and the pull had changed — not a tug anymore but a hum, a resonance, as though the thing inside her had found what it was looking for and was settling into the frequency of it.

She was standing at the edge of a shallow hollow in the grey plain. The stone beneath her feet was warm and scored with patterns she didn’t recognise — spirals and branching lines that looked almost like the pattern on her palm, almost like the thorns she’d seen in the river. The air here tasted different. Sharper. More metallic. And beneath the hum in her chest, beneath the warmth and the pull and the wrongness of everything, she could feel something else — a vibration, low and deep, not in her ears but in her bones, in the ground itself, as though the earth beneath her feet was humming a single, sustained note.

The earth was singing.

She didn’t know how she knew that. But she knew it the way she knew her own name, the way she knew that the sky should be blue and rain should fall downwards and mothers should not walk away in the rain and never come back. The earth was singing, and it was sick, and it was tired, and it had been singing for a very long time, and no one was listening.

And then, from the shadows at the edge of the hollow, a voice. Low. Flat. Empty of everything.

“What are you?”

She turned. And saw him.

* * *

He had been watching her for eleven steps.

She had not seen him. She was too busy falling and stumbling and talking to herself — he could hear her, even at this distance; the Wold carried sound strangely, bending it, stretching it, delivering whispers from metresaway and swallowing shouts whole. Her voice was sharp, accented, human, and it carried the particular quality of someone who used words as weapons because silence was too honest. He recognised the type. He had been the type, once, before silence became preferable.

She was human. That much was obvious. The pallor, the fragility of the bone structure, the way she moved — clumsily, heavily, a creature of solid matter in a world where matter behaved differently. Humans did not belong in Vaelthorn. They passed through thin places by accident, by bargain, by ritual, and almost all of them died within hours, because Vaelthorn was not kind to soft things and humans were the softest things there were.

But the Rootsong was pulsing around her like a heartbeat around a wound, and that was not something the Rootsong did for humans.

He stood in the shadow of a formation of dark stone at the hollow’s edge — the Whispering Wold was full of such formations, remnants of pre-fae geology that no one had ever adequately explained — and he watched her and he did not move. He had not moved in eleven days, not from the Pavilion, not from the terrace, not from the spot where he knelt beside the Thornheart sapling and counted its leaves. He had spoken to no one in eleven days. He had not needed to. The Pavilion was his and the Thornwall was his and the slow, grinding silence of his exile was the only companion he required or deserved.

The Rootsong had changed that.

It had started as a tremor — not physical, but something deeper, a shift in the dreaming consciousness beneath the earth, the vast and ancient thing that had created Vaelthorn and sustained it and was now, slowly and irrevocably, dying. He had felt tremors before. The Rootsong’s decline was measured in such tremors — small stutters in the magic that sustained the realm, brief flickers in the light of the Gilded Hollow, the slow greying of moss that had once burned gold. But this was different. This was not a decline. This was a surge.

The thin place had activated. He had felt it from the Pavilion — a tearing, a rending, a boundary between worlds flexing open like a wound. And through it, something had come. Not a fae. Not a creature of the Thornwall. A human woman, tumbling through the air like a bird with broken wings, hitting the ground of the Whispering Wold with the particular graceless impact of a body that was not designed for this world.

And the Rootsong had pulsed for her.

He did not understand it. Three hundred and ninety-two years had given him a great deal of experience with things he did not understand, and he had learned that the wise response to incomprehension was patience. Watch. Wait. Let the thing reveal itself before acting. Action born of confusion was the province of the young and the desperate, and he was neither, though the desperate part was open to debate depending on how honestly he was willing to examine the last two centuries.

She was not honest with himself often.

The Thornheart sapling had lost another leaf this morning. That made eleven. It had been twenty-three when he had taken up residence at the Pavilion. The last First Tree remnant, dying by inches, and he could not touch it because touch was a weapon and the only safety was distance, and so he watched it die the way he watched everything die, which was with the careful, deliberate emptiness of a man who had decided that caring was too expensive and grief was a bill he could no longer afford to pay.

He had not always been this way.

He remembered — dimly, the way one remembers a life lived in a different body — being young. Being social. Believing the Court could reform, that the rot could be halted, that the Sundering was a problem to be solved rather than a wound to be survived. He had commanded battalions. He had eaten in halls. He had laughed, once, at something someone said across a table, and the sound had surprised him because it had been real.

Veyra had cured him of that.

Sixty years. Sixty years of what he had thought was love, and what had actually been extraction — a Hollow Circle blood mage, harvesting his shadow magic through manufactured intimacy, through touch, through the deliberate and systematic weaponisation of the one thing he had given freely. Sixty years of hands on his skin that were taking, always taking, and him not knowing, not suspecting, because he had believed — genuinely, foolishly, devastatingly — that she loved him. That touch could be something other than a transaction. That someone could reach for him and want nothing in return.

The Ashveil Lantern had shown him the truth. The hollow spaces where his magic had been drained. The years of power he had given away, one touch at a time, to someone who had been calculating his value from the first moment she saw him.

He had killed her in the Thornwall campaigns. It had not helped.

Two hundred and twelve years. Two hundred and twelve years in the Pavilion. Two hundred and twelve years without a hand on his skin, without a voice in his ear, without the particular violation of someone else’s warmth against his own. He had made himself into a shadow because shadows could not be touched, could not be reached, could not be hurt. And it had worked. He had not been hurt in two hundred and twelve years. He had not been anything in two hundred and twelve years, which was the same thing, which was the point.

And now the Rootsong was pulsing, and a human woman was standing in the Whispering Wold, and the earth was singing in a way it had not sung since before the Sundering, and something inside him — something he had buried so deeply that he had forgotten it existed — was stirring.

He did not move. He watched. He waited.

“What are you?” he said.

She turned. And for the first time in two hundred and twelve years, KaelenDuskveil looked at another person and felt something other than nothing.

It was not warmth. It was not welcome. It was recognition — a bone-deep, involuntary recognition of something in her posture, in the set of her jaw, in the way she held herself like someone bracing for impact. She was afraid. She was furious. She was standing in a world she did not understand and she was not going to show it, and beneath the anger and the defiance and the sharp, bright armour of her voice, she was alone. Not alone the way he was alone, not by choice, not by design, but alone the way a person is alone when they have been abandoned so many times that solitude has become the only predictable thing in their life.

He knew that shape. He had worn it himself, once, a very long time ago.

It did not matter. Whatever she was, whoever she was, she did not belong here, and the Rootsong’s interest in her was a problem he did not need. He had enough problems. The Thornwall was advancing. The Pavilion was being consumed. The sapling was dying. The Regent was playing games whose stakes he did not care to calculate. The last thing he required was a human woman in the Whispering Wold and a dreaming god that had decided to wake up.

The gateway she had come through was still visible behind her — a faint shimmer in the air, a wound that was trying to close. He could see the human world through it, dim and fragmented: the grey suggestion of buildings, the sound of water, the smell of rain on tarmac and chip shop grease and all the small, human things that had no place here. The rent was shrinking. In moments it would seal. She would be trapped.

He should have felt something about that. Pity, perhaps. Or the cold satisfaction of a problem solving itself. What he felt was the pull in his chest, the Rootsong’s pulse, and a deep, irrational certainty that letting the gateway close would be wrong.

He hated certainty. Certainty was a luxury for people who believed in things.

The gateway shrieked. Not a sound — a frequency, a vibration that bypassed his ears and went directly to something older, something that lived in his blood and his bones and the shadow-magic that was woven into the fabric of who he was. The rent in the air was not closing neatly. It was collapsing. The edges buckled, twisted, and the light bleeding through it shifted from the soft grey of a human evening to something sharper, angrier, the colour of a fresh bruise.

“The gateway is destabilising,” he said.

It was the first time he had spoken in eleven days, and his voice sounded foreign to him, dry and rusted, like a gate that had not been opened in years.

* * *

“The gateway is destabilising,” he said again, louder now, stepping out of the shadow of the stone formation. “Move.”

“I don’t know what that means.”

“It means the boundary between your world and mine is collapsing, and when it goes, everything within twenty metres will—”

The gateway detonated.

Not an explosion. Not in the way human weapons exploded. But a release — of pressure, of force, of something that had been held between two worlds and was now being expelled from both. The shockwave was invisible but absolute. It hit Seren like a wall and threw her sideways, and she hit the ground hard, the impact driving the air from her lungs, and she felt something in her shoulder tear — not a clean cut, not a blade, but a jagged rip, a shard of something that had been part of the collapsing gateway, sharp and hot and buried in the meat of her shoulder, and the blood was immediate and dark and wrong, too dark, almost black, and it ran down her arm and dripped from her fingers into the grey grass.

Kaelen moved.

Not toward Seren — toward the gateway. The collapsing thin place was not just releasing energy; it was shedding fragments of the boundary itself, and some of those fragments were spiralling toward the Thornwall, and if corrupted Thornwall material absorbed boundary fragments the consequences would be catastrophic. He shadow-stepped. Three steps. The first took him to the gateway’s edge. The second put his hand on the largest fragment — a shard of something between glass and light, hot enough to sear his palm. The third —

The third didn’t complete.

The gateway’s collapse was not linear. It bucked, spasmed, and from its dying throat something lashed out — not a thorn, not a vine, but a strand of the boundary itself, frayed and wild, and it caught him across the chest. Not the old wound on his forearm. A new wound — the strand tore across his ribs, through the fabric of his coat, through the skin beneath, and the pain was immediate and bright and enormous, and the Thornwall cut on his forearm — the one that would not heal, the one that throbbed with corruption — opened with it, as though the new injury had disturbed whatever darkness the thorns had left behind in his blood.

He staggered. Blood — dark, almost black, laced with the faint luminescence of corrupted magic — seeped through his coat and the bandage on his forearm, and the gateway gave one final, tearing shriek and collapsed entirely, leaving behind nothing but a patch of scorched grey grass and a silence that felt like a held breath.

Seren was on the ground. She could see him — the tall figure in black, swaying, one hand pressed to his ribs where blood was spreading across dark fabric, the other hanging at his side where the bandage on his forearm was darkening. The grey grass around him was stained with something that glistened in the amber light.

She should not have moved.

Every survival instinct she had — honed by twenty-four years of keeping herself alive in a world that had not, in her estimation, done much to deserve the effort — told her to stay exactly where she was. This was not her world. This was not her problem. The man in front of her was not her responsibility. She was bleeding from a shoulder that was on fire and her hands were shaking and she was in a world where the sky was the wrong colour and the ground sang and the shadows moved when there was nothing to cast them.

She got up.

She got up because Seren Ashwood’s first response to something terrifying was not to run but to confront it, because running meant admitting she was afraid, and she was afraid, she was terrified, but she was not going to lie in the grey grass and wait for something to happen to her. She had been lying down when her mother left. She had been lying down when her father drank himself into silence. She had been lying down for twenty-four years and she was done with it.

She crossed the distance between them in six steps. He was taller than her by nearly a foot. Up close, she could see his face properly — cold marble skin that seemed to absorb the light rather than reflect it, black hair past his jaw, and eyes that were not eyes, not quite, pale silver with no visible pupil, faintly luminescent in the amber gloom, and they were looking at her with an expression that contained no warmth and no welcome and no softness of any kind, only a flat, assessing calm that was somehow worse than hostility because it meant he was measuring her and finding her insignificant.

“Your wound,” she said.

Stupid. The first words she had spoken to the first person she’d met in an alien world, and they were “your wound.” She was losing blood. She was aware of this in a distant, clinical way — the warmth running down her arm, the sticky wetness on her fingertips, the growing lightness in her head that was not the lightness of relief but the lightness of a body that was running out of what it needed to keep functioning.

“I am aware of it,” he said.

She reached for his forearm — automatic, instinctive, the same reflex that made her right fallen coats and feed strays and pick up the things other people dropped — and he recoiled.

Not a flinch. A full-body recoil, violent and immediate, as though she had raised a blade. The shadows around him surged, thickening, darkening, and she saw his jaw tighten and the silver of his eyes flare bright and the air between them became dense with the pressure of something enormous being restrained.

“Do not touch me.”

Three words. Quiet. The quiet of something that had not spoken in eleven days and had not been touched in two hundred and twelve years and did not intend to start now.

“I’m not going to hurt you.”

Even as she said it she knew how it sounded — how it always sounded when she said things like this, like a challenge wrapped in kindness, like a dare disguised as comfort. She couldn’t help it. She didn’t know how to be gentle. She only knew how to be fierce and hope the other person didn’t mistake it for cruelty.

“I did not ask for your help.”

“No. You didn’t.”

The world tilted. Her knees — her treacherous, shaking knees — buckled, and she was falling, and she put out her hand to catch herself, and her palm — slick with her own blood, dark and wrong and warm — landed on his forearm. His wounded forearm. The one with the Thornwall cut, the one where the bandage had soaked through, where corrupted blood was seeping to the surface, and her palm pressed against the wound and the bloods met.

His blood. Her blood. The boundary’s wound.

Something screamed.

Not either of them. Something beneath them. Something enormous and ancient and alive, something that had been dreaming for millennia beneath the crust of a dying world, and it woke.

Not fully. Not yet. But enough.

The bond hit Seren like a physical blow.

It was behind her sternum — a hook, a hand, something that reached inside her chest and grabbed hold of something she didn’t know she had and pulled. Not outward. Inward. The hook buried itself in the space where the warmth had been, where the thorn’s dust had settled, and it anchored there, and suddenly she was aware of another heartbeat. Not her own. Someone else’s. Slow, strong, ancient, measured — a heartbeat that had been beating for nearly four centuries, steady as a clock, relentless as the tide. And beneath the heartbeat, something else. An emotion. Not hers. A vast, cold, suffocating panic — not the panic of someone facing immediate danger but the panic of something that had been walled away for two hundred years and had just been breached, and the walls were falling, and everything behind them was pouring through.

She gasped. Her hand was still on his forearm. She could feel his skin — cold marble, colder than it should be, colder than any human skin — and beneath it the wound, and the blood, and the place where her blood and his blood had met and something had —

She snatched her hand away.

The bond did not release. The hook behind her sternum held.

Kaelen had gone absolutely still.

Not the controlled stillness of a soldier. Not the measured calm of a man who had spent two centuries perfecting the art of being present without being involved. Something deeper. Something that looked, for one terrible moment, like the edge of an abyss.

He felt it.

He felt the bond — the hook, the anchor, the wire connecting two circuits that were never meant to touch — and he felt it from the other side, and what he felt was not what she felt. What he felt was a door opening in a wall he had spent two hundred and twelve years building, and through the door was light, and warmth, and the overwhelming, suffocating presence of another person’s emotions pressing against his consciousness like a flood against a dam he had thought would hold forever.

Two hundred and twelve years. Two hundred and twelve years of silence and solitude and the careful, deliberate absence of connection, and in one accidental touch it was over.

He could feel her.

Not just her heartbeat — though he could feel that, rapid and furious and young, the heartbeat of someone who had barely begun to live — but the shape of her. The sharp edges of her fear and the sharper edges of her anger and beneath both, buried so deep she probably didn’t know it was there, a vast and aching loneliness that matched the shape of his own like a key in a lock. And other things. Smaller things. The physical sensation of blood running down her arm. The heat of the wound in her shoulder. The faint, fading warmth in her palm where the thorn’s dust had settled.

He knew her. Not her name, not her history, not anything that could be spoken aloud — but the shape of her, the topology of her, the way her emotions moved and shifted and crashed against each other like waves in a storm. It was more intimate than touch. It was more intimate than anything he had experienced in two centuries, and it had happened without his consent, without his knowledge, without the slightest regard for the walls he had built or the price he had paid to build them.

“No,” he said.

It came out broken. The first broken sound he had made in two hundred years.

He shadow-stepped. Ten metres. Fifteen. Twenty. As far as he could go without losing sight of her. The shadows wrapped around him like armour, thick and dense and protective, and he stood in them and felt the bond stretch between them like a wire pulled taut, and the pull in his chest — her direction, her distance, the rough emotional shape of her terror and fury — did not dim. If anything, it was clearer at this distance. Direction. Distance. Emotional state. As though something had installed a compass in his sternum and the only direction it pointed was her.

He could suppress it. He had the skill, the discipline, the centuries of practice at pushing things down. But suppression was a temporary measure and the bond was permanent, and he knew — with the cold, absolute certainty of a man who had studied every form of magic the Court had ever catalogued — that what had just happened was not a spell or a compulsion or anything that could be undone by force of will.

This was the Rootsong.

The Rootsong had forged a bond.

It had been three hundred years since a bond had been forged in Vaelthorn. Queen Mireille had forbidden them after Aldric’s death. The Court feared them, reviled them, killed those who carried them. And the Rootsong — the dying, dreaming consciousness that sustained the realm — had just looked at a human woman and a broken shadow fae and decided, with no consultation and no consent, that they belonged to each other.

Seren stood in the grey grass with blood running down her arm and stared at the place where he had been and then at the place where he was, twenty metres away, wrapped in shadows, his silver eyes burning in the dark, and she felt it — the hook behind her sternum, the pull, the wrongness of another person inside her chest — and she understood with the same gut-level certainty that she understood hunger and exhaustion and love that something had been done to her. Something irreversible. Something that could not be explained or reasoned with or ignored.

She was connected to him.

Not by choice. Not by consent. By blood — her blood on his wound, his blood on her palm, and something ancient and dreaming that had reached up through the ground and forged a chain between two strangers who had not asked for it and did not want it.

“What did you do to me?” she said.

Her voice cracked on the last word. The armour was failing. She could feel it failing — the sharp edges of her anger going blunt, the careful walls she had built crumbling, and beneath them was nothing but the raw, terrified surface of someone who had just been violated in a way she didn’t have a name for.

He looked at her from across twenty metres of grey grass and shadow, and what she saw in his face was not guilt and not sympathy and not explanation. What she saw was the flat, devastated calm of someone whose world had just ended and who was already calculating how to survive the aftermath.

“I did nothing,” he said. His voice was low, measured, empty of everything. “But it appears something else disagrees.”

She didn’t know what he meant. She didn’t know where she was or how she had gotten here or what had just happened inside her chest. She was bleeding from a shoulder wound she couldn’t see, standing in an alien world with a sky the colour of a bruise and a man made of shadows who had just told her that something she couldn’t name had tied them together without asking, and her hand was still warm with his blood, and she could feel his heartbeat in her chest, and she wanted to go home.

“You can’t do this,” she said. “Whatever this is — you can’t just — I didn’t agree to this. I didn’t ask for this. I didn’t —”

“Nor did I.”

The flatness of it stopped her. Not anger. Not argument. A statement of fact, delivered with the weight of two centuries of solitude behind it, and beneath the flatness, the bond pulsed, and she felt what he felt — which was nothing. A vast, careful, deliberate nothing, the nothing of someone who had spent two hundred years learning not to feel and had just discovered that all of it was for nothing.

The nothing was the most terrifying thing she had ever felt. More terrifying than the sky. More terrifying than the wall of thorns. More terrifying than the ground singing beneath her feet. Because she recognised it. She had built her own version of it, brick by brick, year by year, and she knew exactly how much it cost to maintain, and she knew that his version was older and deeper and stronger than hers, and she knew that the bond had just blown a hole in both of them.

The grey grass rippled without wind. The bruised sky pressed down. Somewhere in the distance, the Thornwall creaked and grew, and the thin place’s last traces faded from the scorched earth, and two people who had not chosen each other stood in a dying world and felt the wire between them hum with something that was not quite pain and not quite recognition and was entirely, catastrophically irreversible.

The hook behind Seren’s sternum pulled toward him.

The wire behind Kaelen’s ribs pulled toward her.

Neither moved. Neither spoke. The bond held — a single, sustained note, like the earth’s song, like the hum of something vast and dreaming that had woken for a moment and found what it was looking for and would not let go.

Seren closed her eyes. She was bleeding. She was lost. She was connected to a stranger in a world that was not hers, and the connection was a hook behind her sternum and a heartbeat that was not her own and a loneliness that was not hers but that she recognised like her own reflection.

She opened her eyes.

He was still there. Twenty metres away. Wrapped in shadow. Watching her with silver eyes that held no warmth and no welcome and no sympathy, only the flat, devastated calm of a man who had just lost everything and was already planning how to survive the loss.

They were both aware, with the same terrible certainty, that the bond existed. That neither of them could undo it. That the last thing either of them wanted was the only thing either of them was going to get.

The earth sang. The Thornwall grew. And somewhere, in the space between two heartbeats, something ancient and dreaming settled back into its sleep, satisfied.

title: Chapter 3 — Twenty Meters
content:
He stood twenty metres away and did not come closer.

The shadows around him had thickened since the bond had formed — not a deliberate act, she thought, but an instinct, like a man reaching for a wall when the floor tilts. The amber light of Vaelthorn’s perpetual autumn caught the edges of them and turned them silver, and through the silver she could see the shape of him — tall, angular, black-clad, a blade in silhouette — and the silver eyes that were not quite eyes, watching her with the flat assessment of someone deciding whether a problem was worth solving.

The bond told her things he didn’t say. Direction: east. Distance: nineteen metres, give or take. Emotional state: nothing. Not absence of emotion — nothing. A void so complete it had its own texture, like standing at the edge of a cliff and feeling not the drop but the absence of ground. She had never felt nothing so loudly in her life.

Her shoulder throbbed. The shard of whatever the collapsing gateway had thrown at her was still lodged in the meat, and the blood had crusted dark along her arm, stiffening the fabric of her sleeve. She was losing blood slowly, the kind of steady, undramatic loss that would make her light-headed and stupid if she didn’t do something about it, and she was in an alien world with no phone, no map, no way home, and a stranger who was not coming closer.

“I need you to come here,” she said.

He didn’t move.

“I’m bleeding.”

“I am aware.”

“Then help me.”

“No.”

The word landed like a stone in still water. Not cruel — that would have been easier to handle. Just final. A door closing. The same flat tone he had used when he told her not to touch him, the same emptiness, and beneath it, through the bond, she felt a flicker. Not emotion. The shadow of an emotion, fast and suppressed, the way a fish moves beneath the surface of a frozen lake — visible for an instant in the crack, then gone.

She filed it away. She was good at filing things away. A lifetime of practice.

“Then tell me where I am.”

He regarded her from across the twenty metres of grey grass and scored stone. The Thornwall was visible behind him, a vast black shape on the western horizon, and it moved — she could see it now, thorns the size of trees shifting, reaching, the slow millennial patience of something that had been eating a world for three hundred years. The grey grass rippled away from it. Everything rippled away from it, as though the land itself was trying to flee.

“You are in Vaelthorn,” he said. “The Court of Dusk and Bramble. The gateway through which you arrived has closed. It will not reopen.”

She waited for more. He gave her nothing.

“That’s it?”

“That is the relevant information.”

“Relevant to who?”

He turned. Not toward her — toward the east, toward the shape she could see now on the horizon: a structure, dark against the bruised sky, built into the side of what might have been a cliff or might have been the caldera wall itself. His posture was rigid, controlled, the set of his shoulders the set of someone who was making himself smaller by being stiller.

“You can stay here,” he said, still facing away. “The Wold is not safe after dark. The thorn-wolves hunt in the grey hours. The Hollow Circle uses the Wold as a transit corridor. Without shelter, without knowledge of the terrain, without any capacity to defend yourself, you will die before the next light cycle.”

“Charming.”

“Alternatively,” he said, and the word came out like it was costing him, like each syllable was being extracted under duress, “you can follow me. I have shelter. It is not a gift. It is the practical solution to a problem neither of us asked for.”

She looked at him. At the shadows that clung to him like a second skin. At the blood still seeping through the bandage on his forearm. At the rigidity of his spine and the careful distance he maintained and the way he flinched, microscopically, every time the bond pulsed between them — every time her fear or her fury or her pain bled through the wire and reached him, and he had to feel it, and he had to not respond.

“You could just leave me here,” she said.

He went still. The particular stillness that was not calm but the opposite of calm — the held breath, the braced muscle, the stillness of someone who wants to run and has decided, through force of will, not to.

Through the bond, she felt it again: not emotion, but the pressure of suppressed emotion. A weight behind a door. A door she was not supposed to know about. And something else — brief, involuntary, the ghost of a feeling she couldn’t name but recognised, because it lived in her too. The shape of loneliness so old it had become structural, load-bearing, the thing holding everything else up.

She looked away from him. At the grey grass and the scored stone and the sky the colour of a bruise and the Thornwall, always the Thornwall, creeping closer. At the place where the gateway had been, now nothing but scorched earth and the faint shimmer of boundary remnants, already fading. She thought, fleetingly, of the cottage on the hill in Machynlleth, of Eira’s kitchen with its smell of lavender and dust, of Mei holding a chai latte across the counter and grinning like the world hadn’t gone wrong. The thought was a knife — brief, sharp, gone before she could grab it.

She couldn’t stay here. She knew that the way she knew her own heartbeat — not because anyone had told her, but because her body had figured it out before her mind had caught up. The Wold was not safe. She was wounded. The bond was humming in her chest like a second pulse, and it was pointing toward him, toward the east, toward the dark shape on the horizon, and it was not going to stop.
