“Fine,” she said. “Lead the way.”

He did not look back. He set off toward the east, and she followed, and the distance between them remained constant — twenty metres, give or take, close enough to see but not to touch, close enough for the bond to hum but not to clarify, and Seren limped through an alien landscape with blood on her arm and fury in her chest and a compass behind her sternum that pointed at the only person in this world she didn’t want to be near.

The walk took longer than it should have. The terrain of the Whispering Wold was deceptive — the grey grass hid hollows and ridges and sudden drops, and the light, diffuse and sourceless, made depth perception unreliable. Shadows moved at the edges of her vision. Not his shadows — other shadows, natural ones, the kind that gathered in the folds of the land where the Thornwall’s influence warped the light. She tripped twice. The second time she went down hard on one knee, and the pain in her shoulder flared white, and through the bond she felt his attention sharpen — a brief, involuntary flicker of focus, there and gone, like a searchlight sweeping past and clicking off.

She got up without looking at him. She would not give him the satisfaction.

* * *

She followed at twenty metres.

He had not set that distance deliberately. It was the farthest he could shadow-step and still see her, and he was not going to step closer. The bond did not require proximity — not at this stage, not yet — but it preferred it, and the preference was a pull, a faint, insistent hum behind his ribs that grew louder when she was closer and quieter when she was further and never, ever stopped. He could feel her with the precision of a compass needle: direction, distance, the rough barometric pressure of her emotional state. Anger, mostly. Sharp-edged and brittle, like a blade wrapped in cloth. Fear beneath it, larger and slower, a deep current that ran beneath the anger and surfaced only in moments — when she stumbled, when the Thornwall creaked, when the grey grass rippled toward something she couldn’t see.

He could feel her pain.

Not the shoulder — that was too specific, too physical, too human for the bond to transmit at this stage. But the shape of it. The way it pressed against her consciousness like a weight, colouring everything, turning her anger darker and her fear sharper and her thoughts slower. She was running on adrenaline and fury and not much else, and the adrenaline was fading, and when it went she would crash.

He did not want to feel any of this.

Two hundred and twelve years of silence. Two hundred and twelve years of a space so empty that even sound felt like an intrusion. He had made the Pavilion into a hermitage, a place where nothing reached him and nothing could — no demands, no expectations, no intimacy, no touch. He had done this deliberately, methodically, the way a man boards up a house before a flood: not because he wanted to live in a house with no windows but because the alternative was drowning.

And now the flood was inside his chest.

Every step she took was a sound in a room that had been silent for centuries. The bond didn’t carry sound — it carried the shadow of sound, the emotional residue of a person moving through a space, and Seren Ashwood moved through spaces the way a storm moved through a valley: loudly, disruptively, with a chaos of emotion that his carefully calibrated emptiness had no defence against. She was furious. She was terrified. She was in pain. She was — and this was the worst part, the part that made his self-control cost something it hadn’t cost in two centuries — she was determined. Not broken. Not cowering. Dragging herself across an alien landscape with blood on her arm and demanding, with every ragged step, that the world acknowledge her right to exist in it.

He had not encountered determination in a very long time.

She went down on one knee in a hollow of dark earth, and he felt the spike of pain through the bond like a needle in his own shoulder, and his attention sharpened, and he took half a step toward her before he stopped himself. The half-step was enough. The half-step was a betrayal of everything he had built, every wall, every silence, every year of careful, deliberate distance. He had almost moved toward another person. He had almost reached. The thought made his skin crawl.

He did not reach. He stood in the shadow of a standing stone and watched her get up, and the bond hummed between them with something that was not quite concern and not quite obligation and was entirely unwanted.

The Gilded Hollow came into view as they crested a ridge of dark stone. The caldera opened below them like the palm of a vast hand, and in its centre, ringed by the cracked obsidian spires of the old Court, the Thornwall pressed inward. From this height he could see the full scope of it — not a wall but a net, a web of black thornvines that spread across the landscape like infection, pulsing with the slow, patient rhythm of something alive and hungry. The Court buildings sat in its midst like bones in a throat, half-swallowed, half-resisting. He had watched this view for two centuries. He had catalogued every vine, every tendril, every metre of advance. The Pavilion would be consumed within a decade, perhaps less. He did not care. The Pavilion was a tool. When it was gone, he would find another edge to stand on.

She stopped at the ridge. He felt her stop — the sudden stillness of her, the catch in her breath that translated through the bond as a spike of something that was not quite fear and not quite awe. He did not turn. He kept walking. But he knew what she was seeing, because he had seen it himself every day for two centuries, and it never stopped being terrible.

The Pavilion was not in the Gilded Hollow. It was on the western edge of the caldera, where the Thornwall was closest, where the black vines crept up the stone of the cliff face like fingers feeling for a hold. He had chosen the location deliberately. The reasons were his own.

She followed. She did not comment on the Pavilion when she saw it. He had expected commentary — questions, demands, the sharp tongue he had glimpsed in the Wold. But she was quiet as they approached, and the bond told him why: exhaustion. The adrenaline was gone. The fury was still there but it was thinner now, worn down by blood loss and the relentless strangeness of everything she was seeing and feeling. Her shoulder had stopped bleeding freely — crusted over, the shard still embedded — but the arm hung wrong, and every step cost her.

He stopped at the Pavilion’s entrance. A narrow arch of dark stone, no door, shadow pooled in the threshold like standing water. He did not enter. He stood to one side and let the shadows wrap around him and waited for her to reach him.

Twenty metres. She closed it to fifteen. To ten. To five. The bond sharpened with every step, the hum behind his ribs becoming a resonance, and he felt her emotions with a clarity that was almost unbearable — not specific feelings but their shape, their weight, the topography of her inner life laid bare in emotional contour lines. Pain, exhaustion, the residual heat of anger, and beneath it all, vast and deep and old, the wound that her entire personality had been built around. Abandonment. The knowledge that people left. The certainty that it was safer not to need them.

He knew that wound. He knew it the way a man knows the shape of a room he has lived in for centuries — not because anyone had described it to him, but because it was his too.

She stopped three metres from the entrance. Close enough to see him clearly. Close enough for him to see her: the blood-matted hair, the torn sleeve, the grey-green eyes that were too sharp for someone who had lost that much blood, the set of her jaw that said she was not going to ask permission and she was not going to apologise for existing.

“What is this place?” she asked.

“The Dusk Pavilion.”

“That’s a name, not an answer.”

He did not answer. He stepped aside and gestured toward the arch, a minimal movement of his hand that did not bring him any closer to her. The shadows moved with him, thickening, a barrier of darkness between his body and hers.

She looked at the arch. At the darkness beyond it. At the Thornwall, visible above and behind the Pavilion, the black vines reaching over the rooftop like fingers feeling for something they couldn’t quite grasp.

She walked in.

* * *

The Pavilion was not what she had expected.

She didn’t know what she had expected. Something grander, perhaps — a palace, a fortress, the kind of imposing structure that would match the weight of a man who had lived for four centuries and could step through darkness like water. But the Pavilion was small. Quiet. Built from stone so dark it was almost black, veined with something that caught the amber light and glowed faintly, like phosphorescence in a cave. The walls were bare. The floor was stone, worn smooth by centuries of the kind of solitary pacing that comes not from purpose but from restlessness. There were no carpets. No curtains. No colour of any kind.

It smelled of dust and cold stone and something older — not decay, not rot, but the particular mustiness of a place that had been sealed for a very long time. Like opening a door in an old house and finding a room no one had entered in decades. The air was still. The silence was so complete that she could hear her own heartbeat, and behind it, fainter, his — slow and steady and impossibly old, a metronome ticking out the seconds of a life that had been going on for nearly four hundred years.

The bond. She was hearing his heartbeat through the bond. She hadn’t realised that was something it could do.

She pulled her attention back to the room. It was larger than it had looked from outside — or perhaps it only seemed larger because of what it contained, which was nothing. The main room was open, the ceiling high and vaulted, supported by ribs of dark stone that branched like the veins of a leaf. There was a fireplace on the far wall, cold and dark. A table. A single chair. A narrow cot against one wall, stripped to its frame, no blankets, no pillow. The austerity of it was not monkish — monks chose austerity for a reason. This was the austerity of someone who had simply stopped acquiring things because things required maintenance, and maintenance required engagement with the world, and engagement with the world was a door he had closed and boarded and sealed.

She saw this. She saw it the way she saw everything — automatically, involuntarily, reading the space the way she read people, cataloguing the details that others missed. The worn path on the floor between the cot and the doorway. The dust pattern on the table, undisturbed, no object having rested there recently enough to leave a clean circle. The absence of books, of art, of anything that suggested pleasure or curiosity or the small human habit of putting things on surfaces because looking at them made you feel something. The chair faced the window — not a comfortable chair, not a reading chair, just a chair, positioned so that whoever sat in it could see the sky and, beyond it, the Thornwall.

He sat in that chair. He sat in it and looked at the wall of living thorns that was eating the world, and he did this every day, and he had done this for two hundred years, and he had not moved the chair.

She understood, with a clarity that surprised her, that this was not a home. A home implied warmth, comfort, the accumulation of small choices — the colour of a curtain, the position of a lamp, the decision to keep a book or discard it. The Pavilion was not a home. The Pavilion was a monument. A man who had been so deeply hurt that he had built himself a shrine to the absence of everything that could hurt him again, and then he had gone inside and closed the door and stayed there, not because he wanted to live but because living, in the world, with other people, had become unbearable.

The thought made her chest ache. Not the bond — not his pain, not his wound. Hers. The recognition of a shape she knew too well, the shape of someone who had decided that the safest place to be was nowhere, and the safest person to be was no one, and the safest way to live was to stop living and just exist instead.

She had been building her own version of this for years. The difference was that hers was still under construction. His was finished.

She turned to look at him. He had followed her in — at a distance, always at a distance, staying near the entrance as though the room itself was too small to share. His silver eyes tracked her as she moved through the space, and she felt the bond sharpen with each step she took deeper into his territory. She could feel him not wanting her here. Not hatred, not anger — just a vast, hollow resistance, the reflexive rejection of a system that had not processed input from another person in over two centuries.

Through the bond, she caught something she shouldn’t have. A flicker at the edge of his emptiness — not an emotion, exactly, but the memory of one. Old grief. So old it had calcified, turned to stone, become part of the architecture of his emptiness rather than something that moved through it. She caught it for a fraction of a second: the shape of a hand reaching for him in darkness, and the way he had flinched from it, and the terrible cost of flinching from a hand you had once believed meant safety.

It was gone before she could hold it. The emptiness slammed back, like a door closing, and the bond went flat and quiet, and she understood that he had felt her feeling it and had shut her out with the brutal efficiency of someone who had been practising for two hundred years.

“Your shoulder,” he said.

She blinked. The shift from that intimate, involuntary glimpse to his flat, clinical voice was like being pushed underwater. “What?”

“The wound. Sit.”

It was not a request. It was the flat delivery of someone issuing a command to the air, without looking at her, without moving toward her. He nodded toward the chair by the window — his chair, she realised, the one that faced the Thornwall — and then he moved to a low shelf built into the far wall that she hadn’t noticed. He opened a small wooden box without approaching her and withdrew a cloth, a vial of something dark, a thin needle of bone.

She sat. Not because he told her to — though that was the excuse she gave herself — but because her legs had reached the point where standing required more energy than she had left. The chair was uncomfortable. Hard stone, no cushion. She could see why he had chosen it. Comfort was an invitation to stay, and staying was a vulnerability, and vulnerability was a weapon waiting to be used against you.

He set the items on the table. Not in front of her. On the far side. He stepped back. Three metres. The bond hummed between them.

“The shard needs to come out,” he said. “I will not touch you. You will need to do it yourself.”

She looked at the items. At the bone needle. At the dark liquid in the vial. At him, standing three metres away with his arms at his sides and his jaw tight and the shadows gathered around him like witnesses.

“What’s in the vial?”

“Moss extract. It will numb the area and slow the bleeding. It will not heal the wound — healing magic is beyond what this place can provide without access to the Rootsong’s deeper channels, and those channels are corrupted beyond use in this region.”

She picked up the vial. Her hand was shaking. Not from fear — from blood loss, from exhaustion, from the accumulated weight of everything that had happened since the riverbank in Machynlleth, which felt like it had happened in a different life, to a different person. She uncorked the vial and the smell hit her — green and sharp and alive, the smell of the moss she had seen on the Pavilion walls, concentrated and pungent. She poured it over the wound on her shoulder, and the cold was immediate and enormous, spreading from the shoulder across her chest and down her arm in a wave that took the pain with it.

The bone needle was thin and sharp and curved at the tip. She probed the wound until she felt the shard — small, metallic, burning cold even through the numbness — and she gripped it with the needle and pulled. It came free with a small, wet sound, and she dropped it on the table and pressed the cloth to her shoulder and sat very still and breathed.

Through the bond, she felt him watching. Not looking — watching. His attention had a different texture than his other emotions. Sharper. More focused. The emptiness receded when he watched her, replaced by something she couldn’t name, and she caught, briefly, involuntarily, a flicker of something that was not emptiness at all — a flash of old grief, so fast and so suppressed that she might have imagined it, like the impression of a hand in fog.

She pressed the cloth harder. She didn’t ask. She didn’t say anything. She had learned, over twenty-four years, that some doors were not yours to open.

* * *

The terrace was through a low arch at the back of the main room.

She found it because she was looking for a window. The Pavilion was so dark and so still that she needed air, needed space, needed something that wasn’t stone and shadow and the silent, oppressive awareness of the man who stood three metres behind her and radiated the particular energy of someone who was trying very hard not to exist.

The terrace was narrow, cantilevered over the edge of the caldera. The view hit her like a physical thing — the Gilded Hollow spread below, cracked and tarnished, its obsidian spires catching the amber light, and beyond them, the Thornwall. From here she could see the full horror of it: not a single wall but a sea of black thornvines that spread from the western horizon to the Court’s inner walls, pulsing with the slow, patient rhythm of something alive and eating. The closer vines were skeletal, leafless, reaching over the Pavilion’s rooftop. She could hear them — a faint creaking, like old wood in wind, except there was no wind and these were not trees.

She looked at the Thornwall and understood, in the place beneath understanding, that this world was dying. Not metaphorically. Not slowly. Actively, visibly, the way a body dies — consumed from the outside by something that had no intention of stopping until there was nothing left to consume.

And he had chosen to live next to it.

Not behind it. Not away from it. Next to it. Close enough to hear it breathing. Close enough to reach out and touch it, if he wanted to, if touch were something he still did, which it was not. He had built his shrine to emptiness on the edge of the thing that was killing the world, and he sat in his hard chair and looked at it every day, and she did not understand why but she understood the shape of the gesture, because she had made gestures like it herself — choosing the painful thing, the close thing, the thing that reminded you every day of what you had lost, because the alternative was forgetting, and forgetting felt like betrayal.

She turned from the Thornwall. And saw the sapling.

It was in the corner of the terrace, in a shallow bed of dark soil that looked dry and cracked and half-dead. The tree itself was small — barely taller than she was, thin-trunked, its branches sparse and bare except for the leaves. The leaves. There were eleven of them. She counted them without meaning to, the way you count the petals of a dying flower or the remaining beats of a failing heart. Eleven leaves, and each one was wrong — a colour that couldn’t decide what it was, gold gone grey, green gone dim, the faded memory of something that had once been vivid and alive and was now clinging to existence through sheer, stubborn refusal to stop.

It was the saddest thing she had ever seen.

Not because it was ugly. It wasn’t. There was a beauty in it — the grace of the branching, the delicate architecture of the trunk, the way the remaining leaves caught the amber light and held it like something precious. It was the sadness of a thing that was trying. That was still trying, despite everything. Despite the dying world and the poisoned earth and the centuries of neglect. Eleven leaves. It was down to eleven leaves and it was still standing.

She looked at Kaelen. He was standing in the archway behind her, at the threshold, not on the terrace. Three metres. His silver eyes were on the sapling, and on his face was an expression she had not seen before — not emptiness, not flatness, but something raw and exposed and quickly buried, like a wound reopening and being pressed shut in the same instant.

He tended this. The man who wouldn’t be touched, who had sealed himself in a stone box for two centuries, who flinched when she reached for him and spoke in a voice that had rusted from disuse — he tended a dying tree. He could not touch it — she could see that, see the careful distance he maintained from it, the way he positioned himself near it but never close enough to brush against it, as though even the idea of touching something this fragile was more than he could bear. But he was here. Every day. Tending. The soil was turned — recently, she could see the marks of a tool in the dry earth. The trunk was clean, free of the dark growth that she had seen on other plants in the Wold, carefully scraped away. The bed was weeded, the few surviving fungi cleared, the stones arranged to catch runoff from the caldera wall.

He could not touch it. But he would not let it die alone.

The thought landed in her chest and stayed there, and she did not know what to do with it, so she did what she always did with things she didn’t know what to do with: she filed it away and said nothing and let her face show nothing and hoped that the bond was not transmitting the ache that the thought had left behind.

Through the bond, she felt a flicker. Not an emotion — a suppression. The sense of a door closing, quickly and quietly, on a room she was not supposed to see. He had felt her seeing. He had felt her understanding. And he was shutting it out, the way he shut everything out, the way he had been shutting everything out for two hundred years, and the efficiency of it was almost admirable if it hadn’t been so devastating.

She turned back to the Thornwall. The bruised sky pressed down. The sapling stood in its corner, eleven leaves holding on. The bond hummed between her ribs and his — two compasses pointing at each other, two heartbeats that were not supposed to be connected, two people who had built their lives around the principle that needing was dangerous and being needed was worse, and were now trapped inside each other’s emotional radius whether they liked it or not.

She did not like it. She could feel, with the same bone-deep certainty that she felt her own name, that he did not like it either. But the bond was a fact, and the Pavilion was a fact, and the sealed gateway was a fact, and all the fury in the world was not going to change any of them.

She pressed her hand to her shoulder, where the moss extract had gone cold and the shard-wound was a dull, persistent throb. Her fingers came away tacky with dried blood. She needed to change the cloth. She needed to rest. She needed to find a way home that probably didn’t exist.

Instead, she stood on the terrace of a dying man’s tomb and looked at his dying tree and felt his dying heartbeat through a wire that neither of them had asked for, and the Thornwall creaked, and the sky darkened, and Vaelthorn turned slowly, slowly in its perpetual autumn, and no one came to help, and no one was going to, and the only person in this world she could feel was the last person in this world she wanted.

The bond held. The sapling held. The Pavilion held its breath.

Inside, in the room with the hard chair and the bare walls and the dust on the table, there was a cot. She would sleep there, because she had no choice. He would not sleep at all, because he hadn’t in two centuries, and having someone in his space was a species of noise he had forgotten how to filter out.

The Thornwall grew. The leaves held. Eleven.

title: Chapter 4 — The Wrong Sky
content:
She woke to the wrong sky.

The Pavilion ceiling was dark stone, veined with phosphorescence, and above the vaulted ribs of it the sky showed through a gap she hadn’t noticed the night before — not a window but a crack in the roof, or perhaps the roof had been built that way, open to the bruised amber of Vaelthorn’s perpetual autumn. There was no sunrise. The light simply shifted, deepening from purple-black to amber-grey, the way a bruise shifts from purple to yellow as it heals. She did not know what time it was. She did not know if time worked the same way here. The cot was hard beneath her, the moss-extract numbness had worn off, and her shoulder was a deep, persistent throb that sat in the meat of her like something that had taken up residence and intended to stay.

The bond was still there.

She had hoped, in the irrational way you hope for things while falling asleep in an alien world, that it might have been a dream. That she would wake up in Eira’s cottage with the smell of lavender and the sound of rain and the normal, boring, precious weight of being exactly where she was supposed to be. But the hook was behind her sternum, the pull was pointing east, and somewhere in the Pavilion, on the other side of the stone wall, she could feel him. Not his thoughts. Not his words. Just his shape — the vast, flat emptiness of him, the particular quality of nothing that was not absence but a presence so controlled it had become indistinguishable from absence.

He was awake. She could tell because the emptiness had a texture when he was awake that it didn’t have when he was — no. She didn’t know if he slept. The spec sheet on that was: two hundred and twelve years of silence probably meant two hundred and twelve years of insomnia, and she was not going to investigate further because investigating meant paying attention to the bond, and paying attention to the bond meant accepting it, and accepting it was not on the list of things she was prepared to do.

She sat up. The room spun briefly. She pressed her hand to her shoulder and the wound was hot and tight and crusted with dried blood, and the cloth she’d pressed against it had stuck to the dried edges and pulling it free was a small, sharp, undignified pain that she dealt with the way she dealt with most pain: by ignoring it and doing the next thing anyway.

The next thing was: stand up. The next thing after that was: find water. The next thing after that was: figure out where she was and how to get out and what the fuck was happening and why the ground was singing and the sky was bruised and she could feel a stranger’s emotional weather through a wire in her chest.

She stood. The room wobbled. She waited for it to stop. It didn’t, exactly, but it became manageable, the way seasickness becomes manageable if you’re on a boat long enough — not gone, but integrated, a background hum that your body learns to work around.

The Pavilion was different in the not-morning. Quieter, if that was possible. The amber light through the roof-g crack fell in a long diagonal across the stone floor, picking out the dust motes, the worn path between the cot and the doorway, the single chair by the far wall. His chair. Empty now. He was not in the main room.

The terrace. The bond told her he was on the terrace.

She did not go to the terrace. She went to the archway that led to the main entrance and stood in it and looked out at the Whispering Wold and the grey grass rippling without wind and the Thornwall on the western horizon, closer than it had been yesterday — she was sure of that, though she had no way to measure, no reference point, no normal against which to calibrate. It was like watching a tide come in. Each time she looked, the black mass of thornvines seemed larger, more intricate, more alive. It creaked. The sound carried across the Wold like the creak of a ship’s hull in a swell, and it was the loneliest sound she had ever heard, because it was the sound of a world dying in slow motion and there was nothing she could do about it.

She pressed her back against the cool stone of the archway and tried to think. Her mind, normally sharp and orderly, felt like a room that had been ransacked — everything was there but nothing was where it was supposed to be. She was in a world that shouldn’t exist. She was bonded to a man who didn’t want her. She was wounded and alone and the only gateway home had sealed behind her like a wound closing.

Her shoulder throbbed. The bond hummed. The Thornwall creaked.

She was still trying to formulate a plan — something more coherent than survive, something that involved answers and explanations and a way home — when she felt the change through the bond.

It was subtle. A shift in the texture of the emptiness. The flat, controlled nothing that was KaelenDuskveil sharpened at the edges, became harder, tenser, the way a still body becomes tense when it hears a sound it doesn’t recognise. Something was approaching. He could feel it. Through the bond, so could she.

* * *

He had been on the terrace for an hour.

The ritual was the same every morning. He stood at the edge of the sapling’s bed and did not touch it and counted its leaves. Eleven. The same as yesterday. The same as the day before that, and the day before that, and every day for eleven months since the last leaf had fallen. He counted them because counting was the only form of care he permitted himself, and because the day he stopped counting would be the day he stopped caring, and stopping caring would mean the isolation had finally finished what it had started, and he was not ready for that. He was not sure he would ever be ready for that.

The soil was dry. He had watered it three days ago with the runoff from the caldera wall — collected in a stone basin, carried with his shadows rather than his hands, poured from a height that kept his fingers a foot from the earth. The water had not helped. Nothing helped. The Rootsong was failing and the sapling was dying and he could not touch it and could not heal it and could not do anything except stand here every morning and count its leaves and pretend that the counting was enough.

The bond hummed. She was awake. He felt her stir on the other side of the wall — the disorientation, the spike of pain, the brief irrational hope that the bond had been a dream, the cold acceptance when it wasn’t. Her emotions in the morning were louder than in the evening. Rawer. The sharp tongue was still in its sheath; what the bond picked up was the animal beneath it, the frightened, furious thing that had not yet assembled its defences.

He did not think about this. He turned his attention to the Thornwall and the caldera and the slow grey advance of rot, and he let his emptiness do what it had done for two centuries: fill the space where feeling should have been with a weight so dense nothing could penetrate it.

It worked. Mostly.

The change came from the east.

He felt it before he saw it — a shift in the air, a pressure, the particular quality of movement that meant bodies approaching the Pavilion through the Wold. Not one body. Several. The cadence was military: measured, disciplined, the rhythm of people who had been trained to move together. He had been military once. He recognised the cadence the way you recognise a language you used to speak.

His self-control did not waver. His emptiness did not crack. But something behind the emptiness shifted — not an emotion, not even the memory of one, but a structural change, like the frame of a house settling under a new weight. Someone from the world outside the Pavilion was approaching, and the last time someone from the world outside the Pavilion had approached, the bond hadn’t existed, and the space had been his alone, and that had been the whole point.

They came around the caldera edge in formation — four soldiers in the dark iron-and-leather of House Ironveil, the crossed-sword-and-shield sigil on their chest plates, thorn-iron weapons at their belts. They moved with the compact precision of people who expected resistance and were prepared to meet it. Behind them, one figure walking not with the formation but with the easy authority of someone who led formations rather than followed them.

He knew who it was before the figure came close enough for his eyes to confirm. The bond told him — not through its emotional barometer but through his reaction to it. The emptiness, which had been flat and controlled for two centuries, went hard. The way steel goes hard when it’s quenched: not changed in temperature, not altered in composition, but fundamentally different in its structure. Something had been reinforced. Something had been braced.

Commander TherynIronveil stopped ten metres from the Pavilion entrance. The soldiers fanned out behind her in a loose semicircle — not aggressive, but not casual either. The positioning of people who understood that a cornered thing was a dangerous thing and had no intention of becoming a lesson in why.

She was tall — nearly his height — and broad across the shoulders in the way of someone who had spent centuries swinging a blade. Close-cropped silver hair, weathered face, steady grey eyes that assessed the Pavilion and the Thornwall and the caldera edge with the automatic sweep of a soldier reading terrain. Her arms, below the rolled sleeves of her commander’s coat, were mapped in old scars — Thornwall marks, pale ridges of healed tissue that caught the amber light like topography. She was three hundred and eighteen years old and she looked it the way a blade looks after centuries of use: worn, but not dulled.

She looked at him. He looked at her. Neither moved.

Through the bond, he felt Seren’s reactions — the spike of alertness when she sensed the approach, the sharpening of fear when soldiers appeared, the hot edge of her fury rising in response to the threat. Her emotions were loud — they were always loud, a chaos of feeling that his carefully calibrated emptiness had no protocol for processing. She was standing in the archway of the Pavilion entrance, he could feel her exact position through the bond, and she was watching the soldiers with the particular expression of someone who was calculating exits and deciding whether fighting was stupider than running.

He had his own calculations to make.

“Commander.” The word came out flat. Not cold — flat. Two hundred years of practice.

“Warden.” Theryn’s voice was low, controlled, the voice of someone who had spent three centuries giving orders and receiving them. She did not smile. She did not frown. Her face held the particular neutrality of a weapon still in its sheath. “I need to speak with you.”

“You are speaking with me.”

“I need to speak with you inside. And with the human.”

The word human landed in the space between them like a stone. It was not an insult — Theryn was too professional for that — but it was a designation, a classification, and it told him that she knew what he was sheltering and had come prepared for it.

He did not ask how she knew. He did not need to. The bonding had disturbed the Rootsong. The Rootsong was the Regent’s to monitor. If a disturbance large enough to register had occurred, the Regent would have felt it, and the Regent’s response to anything he felt was to send Theryn. This was the way it had always been. The Regent measured. Theryn delivered. The world turned.

“The Pavilion is small,” he said. “Your soldiers can wait outside.”

Theryn studied him. The grey eyes moved across his face with the efficiency of a military assessment — checking for changes, for weakness, for anything that had shifted in the two centuries since she had last stood close enough to see. He let her look. His emptiness held.

Two soldiers took positions at the entrance. The other two held the perimeter. Theryn walked into the Pavilion as though she had been there before — which she had, once, a very long time ago — and stood in the centre of the main room and looked at the bare walls and the single chair and the dust on the table, and he watched her read the space the way Seren had read it, except Theryn did not read it as a monument. She read it as a tactical position. A stronghold. A man who had chosen his ground and fortified it.

Her assessment lasted four seconds. Then she turned to the archway where Seren was standing.

Through the bond, he felt Seren’s fear sharpen into something harder. Not bravery — Seren would have called it that, but he recognised it as the same instinct that had made her reach for his wounded arm in the Wold: the refusal to be small, the insistence on being present even when presence cost her everything. She was scared. She was furious. She was not going to hide.

* * *

The woman in the Pavilion was the most terrifying person Seren had ever seen.

Not because she was threatening her. She wasn’t — not directly. She was just standing in the centre of the room with her hands at her sides and her scarred arms exposed and her grey eyes moving, and the way she occupied the space made Seren feel like a small animal in a room with something that ate small animals for breakfast but had already eaten and wasn’t hungry. There was no malice in it. That was what made it terrifying. This was not personal. This was professional.

The soldiers at the entrance were worse. They stood on either side of the arch like pillars, in their dark iron-and-leather, and they did not look at her and they did not need to. Their presence was the message. You are here and we are here and the difference between us is that we chose to be.

Through the bond, she could feel Kaelen. He had come in from the terrace and was standing near the far wall, three metres from Theryn, his silver eyes fixed on the commander with an expression that she had learned, over the past day, to read as the opposite of calm. His calm was a performance. His emptiness was a wall. And right now the wall was costing him more to maintain than she had seen it cost before.

Something about this woman was cracking his control.

Not visibly. His face was stone. His posture was stone. But the bond carried what his face didn’t: a hardness, a brittleness, the particular quality of something that was about to shatter and was holding itself together through sheer, accumulated habit. She didn’t understand it. She didn’t know who this woman was or what history they shared. But she could feel the weight of it in the space between them, and the weight was enormous.

“Seren Ashwood.” Theryn said it like she was reading it from a file. “Twenty-four. Human. Arrived through a thin place in the Whispering Wold approximately eighteen hours ago. Wounded in the collapse.”

Seren stared at her. “You know my name.”

“I know your name, your species, your age, your point of entry, and the approximate time of your arrival. I know that the thin place through which you came is now sealed. I know that you are bonded to the Warden of the Dusk Pavilion. I know that the bonding was detected by the Regent. What I do not know is how you feel about any of this, and that is the only piece of information in this room that interests me.”

Seren opened her mouth. Closed it. Opened it again. The woman had delivered all of that in the same tone a doctor might use to describe a rash — clinical, precise, stripped of everything except fact — and Seren, who had spent her entire life being the sharpest person in the room, had nothing. No quip. No deflection. Just the raw, exposed feeling of being seen by someone who had no interest in her comfort.

“How do you know all that?” she managed.

“The Regent monitors the Rootsong. The bonding registered as a disturbance. I was dispatched to assess.”

“The Regent.” The word was foreign in her mouth. “Who is the Regent?”

Theryn looked at her. The grey eyes held hers, and for a moment Seren felt the full weight of three centuries of military authority pressing against her like a hand on her sternum. Not hostile. Not kind. Just vast.

“Lord VaelDuskfire,” Theryn said. “Head of House Dusk. Ruler of the Court of Dusk and Bramble. He has been aware of your presence in Vaelthorn since the moment you arrived. He wishes to see you.”

“He wishes to —” Seren stopped. She was aware that her voice was rising, and she didn’t care. She was aware that she was in an alien world with a bonded stranger and a military commander and four soldiers and no way home, and the only power she had left was the power of not being quiet. “I don’t know who the Regent is. I don’t know what the Court is. I don’t know why a bonding — whatever that means — registered on anything, and I don’t understand why any of this is any of his business.”

“It is his business because it happened in his realm,” Theryn said. “And because the bonding disturbed the Rootsong, which is the foundation of everything in Vaelthorn. And because you are human, which means you do not belong here, which means your presence is by definition a concern of the Court.”

Each clause landed like a nail being hammered. Seren felt them go in. She didn’t have a defence — not against this. Theryn was not being cruel. She was being precise. And precision, when it came from someone with this much authority, was its own kind of violence.

Through the bond, she felt Kaelen’s reaction. Not the words — the words were his, controlled and empty as always. But underneath, a strain. A pressure. The effort of standing in a room with someone from his past and maintaining the wall while simultaneously processing her — Seren’s — fear and fury through the bond. He was being squeezed from both sides, and the squeezing was costing him something she couldn’t see but could feel, a faint tremor in the wire between them, a hairline crack in the emptiness.

“I’m not going anywhere with you,” Seren said.

She said it to Theryn but she felt it land in Kaelen’s chest through the bond, and she caught, involuntarily, the ghost of something that was not emptiness — a flicker of surprise, maybe, or recognition, or the exhausted appreciation of someone who had just heard another person refuse something and had forgotten, in two centuries of solitude, what that sounded like.

It was gone before she could hold it.

“The Warden will decide what he wishes to do,” Theryn said, and turned to Kaelen, and the weight of her attention shifted from Seren to him with the ease of someone who had been deciding which problem to address first for three centuries. “The Regent’s summons is not a request, Warden. You know this.”

* * *

He knew.

He had known since the moment the bonding had registered, since the Rootsong had pulsed and the disturbance had rippled outward through the dreaming consciousness of the earth and every sufficiently powerful fae in the Court had felt it. The Regent would feel it first. The Regent felt everything first. And the Regent’s response to feeling something was never patience.

Lord VaelDuskfire had allowed his exile because Kaelen was not causing trouble. A distant branch of House Dusk, quartered at the edge of the caldera, tending a dying tree and bothering no one — the Regent could tolerate that. The Pavilion was politically neutral. Kaelen was politically invisible. The arrangement had worked for two centuries because Kaelen had made sure it worked, had kept his head down and his magic contained and his silence absolute and his existence irrelevant to the intricate machinery of Court politics that ground on without him.

Now he was causing trouble.

The bond was trouble. The human was trouble. The Rootsong’s disturbance was trouble. And trouble, in the Court of Dusk and Bramble, was the one thing the Regent could not afford to ignore.

He could not refuse. That was the trap. Kaelen was House Dusk — distant branch, no political value, but House Dusk nonetheless — and the Regent was the head of House Dusk, and the head of a house could summon any member of that house, and refusal was not a thing that House Dusk members did if they wished to remain House Dusk members. The consequences of defiance would not fall on him. He did not care about consequence. They would fall on Seren. A human with no status, no protection, no knowledge of the world she had stumbled into. The Regent could have her detained, interrogated, disappeared into whatever dark corner of the Court housed the things the Regent preferred not to think about.

He could not refuse because refusing endangered her.

The bond made her his responsibility. Not his choice. Not his desire. His responsibility. A wire connecting two lives, and if one end was pulled, the other followed. The Regent understood this. Theryn understood this. The soldiers at the entrance, standing with the practiced patience of people who had escorted reluctant fae to the Court before, understood this.

“The human is under your protection,” Theryn said. It was not a question.

“The human is bonded to me. That is not the same thing.”

“It is, in the Regent’s eyes, exactly the same thing. You are the Warden. She is in the Pavilion. The Pavilion is House Dusk territory. Everything that happens here is your responsibility, including her.”

The words were precise. Theryn was always precise. She had not come to argue or persuade or negotiate. She had come to deliver a message, and the message was this: the world outside the Pavilion had noticed them, and the world outside the Pavilion was not going to let them stay unnoticed.

He looked at her. Three metres away. Close enough to see the Thornwall scars on her arms, the weathered lines of her face, the steady grey eyes that held no accusation and no warmth. She was a soldier. She had always been a soldier. She looked at him the way she had looked at him at Thornspine Pass, two centuries ago — not as a comrade, not as a friend, but as a tactical asset, something to be deployed and managed and moved to where the battle required him to be.

He had not been to the Court in two hundred and twelve years.

The last time he had stood in the throne room, Mireille had been on the throne and the Regent had been young and the Thornwall had been a distant problem on the horizon and Kaelen had still believed that the world could be fixed by someone willing to fix it. Then Veyra had happened. Then the Pavilion had happened. Then two centuries of silence, measured in fallen leaves and shadow-step distances and the slow, grinding advance of thorns across the caldera floor.

He did not want to go back.

The Court was a place of masks and bargains and the slow weaponisation of intimacy. It was a place where touch was leverage and words were traps and every smile concealed a calculation. He had left it because it had nearly killed him — not physically, but in every other way that mattered — and the Pavilion was the antidote, the place where none of that could reach him, and now Theryn was standing in it, and the bond was humming, and Seren was behind him with her sharp tongue and her sharper fear, and the whole structure of his exile was cracking under the weight of a world that would not let him disappear.

“Theryn.” Her name was the first sound he had made that held any inflection at all. Not warmth. Not anger. Just recognition. The recognition of a name spoken by someone who had not said a name with feeling in a very long time. “You carry this message because he sent you. Not because you believe in it.”

Theryn’s expression did not change. But the silence between them shifted — a fractional easing, the release of pressure in a room that had been pressurised since the moment she had walked in. She had been carrying something, and he had named it, and the naming had let it shift, if only slightly.

“I carry this message because the Regent ordered me to carry it,” she said. “What I believe is not relevant. What is relevant is that the bonding disturbed the Rootsong, and the Regent will have answers. He will have them at the Court, where he can control the information and contain the consequences. He has given you until the next light cycle to present yourself. After that, I am authorised to escort you both, by force if necessary.”

The deadline landed in the room like a blade.

Through the bond, he felt Seren’s fear spike — not at the threat of force but at the finality of it, the click of a door closing, the sense that options were being removed one by one and the last one left was the one she least wanted. He felt her anger, hot and sharp, rising against the fear like a blade against a sheath. He felt her look at him, and in her emotional barometer he read the question she was too proud to ask aloud: are you going to let them take me?

He did not answer. He could not answer. Because the answer was not no.

The silence stretched. Theryn stood in the centre of his Pavilion and waited with the patience of a soldier who had learned, over three centuries, that waiting was a weapon. The soldiers held the entrance. The bond hummed between his ribs and Seren’s. The Thornwall creaked on the horizon.

“I will present myself at the Court,” he said.

The words came out like something being pulled from him. Not surrender — he did not surrender. But the closest thing to it that his self-control would permit. A decision made under pressure, in a room he could no longer protect, with a bond he could not sever and a responsibility he had not chosen.

Theryn nodded. A single, precise movement. “I will return at the next light cycle. Be ready.”

She turned and walked out of the Pavilion. The soldiers followed. Their footsteps faded into the Wold, swallowed by the grey grass and the wrong echoes, and the Pavilion was quiet again, and the quiet was different now, thinner, more fragile, like the silence after a storm has passed and you know another one is coming.

Through the bond, he felt Seren’s fury — not directed at Theryn, not at the soldiers, but at him. At his capitulation. At his quiet acceptance of a summons he had not challenged. She did not understand. She could not understand. She had not spent two hundred years building a fortress and she did not know what it cost to watch someone walk through its walls as though they weren’t there.

He turned to the window. The Thornwall was closer today. He was sure of it.

The sapling held eleven leaves.

* * *

When the soldiers had gone, the Pavilion felt smaller.

Not physically — the space was the same: bare walls, worn floor, one chair, one cot, the faint phosphorescence of the stone veins, the crack in the roof where the wrong sky came through. But something had been taken from the room, and what had been taken was the illusion that the Pavilion was hidden, that they were safe, that the world outside had forgotten them.

The world outside had not forgotten them. The world outside had sent four soldiers and a commander with scars on her arms and a voice like a blade being drawn from a sheath, and the commander had said the Regent wants you, and the Warden had said I will present myself, and the door was closing and the window was closing and the last air was leaving the room and Seren Ashwood was trapped in an alien world with a stranger she was bonded to and a Court she didn’t understand and no way home and no choice and no power except the power of her own fury, which was considerable but not, she was beginning to suspect, enough.

She turned on him.

“You said you would present yourself.”

“I did.”

“You didn’t fight it.”

“No.”

“She walked in here and told you to go and you just — agreed.”

“The Regent’s authority over House Dusk is absolute. I am House Dusk. Refusal would not have changed the outcome. It would only have delayed it and given the Regent cause to act against you directly.”

“Against me.”

“You have no status. No protection. No affiliation. In the eyes of the Court, you are a human who entered Vaelthorn without authorisation and was bonded to a House Dusk warden through means the Court does not yet understand. The Regent could have you detained on those grounds alone. I chose not to give him that reason.”

She stared at him. He was standing at the window, his back to her, the silhouette of him dark against the amber light of the caldera. The Thornwall was visible over his shoulder — vast, black, alive, the thorns reaching toward the Pavilion like fingers toward something they couldn’t quite grasp. His posture was rigid. The shadows around him were thick.

Through the bond, she felt what his posture would not show: not emptiness, not exactly, but the effort of emptiness. The cost of maintaining the wall. Theryn’s arrival had cracked something in him — not visibly, not in any way that would show in his voice or his face, but in the wire between them, the hairline fracture was there, a tremor in the hook behind his sternum, a strain in the direction-compass that pointed at her. He was holding himself together, and the holding was harder than it had been yesterday, and the bond was making sure she knew it.

She did not soften. Softening was a luxury she could not afford in a place where everything she had was being taken from her one piece at a time.

“Who is Theryn?” she asked.

He was quiet for three seconds. Three seconds in which the bond hummed and the Thornwall creaked and she felt him decide what to tell her and what to withhold, the calculation happening in real time behind the wall.

“Commander of House Ironveil. The military arm of the Court. We fought together, once.”

“And now she works for the Regent.”

“She serves the Court. The Regent leads the Court. The distinction matters to her more than it matters to him.”

Something in the way he said it — the cadence, the choice of words, the faint weight on served — told her there was more. There was always more with him, layers of history packed so tightly beneath the surface that she caught glimpses of them through the bond like fossils in cliff faces: shapes, impressions, the outline of something enormous buried under centuries of silence. She did not dig. She had learned, in twenty-four years of reading people, that some fossils were better left in the rock.

She pressed her hand to her shoulder. The wound was a dull throb, hot beneath the dried blood. She needed to clean it. She needed food. She needed answers. She needed, above all else, to feel like she had a choice about something, anything, even if the choice was meaningless.

She chose to sit down.

She sat on the cot — his cot, the one he had given her, the one he didn’t use — and she pressed her back against the cold stone wall and she looked at the bare room and the empty chair and the dust on the table and she understood, with the clarity that came from having nothing left to protect, that the Pavilion had changed. Yesterday it had been a prison. Today it was the only safe space she had, and tomorrow she would have to leave it, and the only person she had in this world was a man who could not touch her and would not look at her and was carrying her toward a Court she didn’t understand because the bond had made her his responsibility and his sense of duty was stronger than his desire to hide.

The bond hummed. The Thornwall grew. The sapling held eleven leaves.

And somewhere, in the Court she could not see and did not understand, the Regent was waiting.
